CHINA TEAS.
Tea a la Sir Andrew Clarke,
For years, whenever my Customers have asked me bra Mild Tea, I have'advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated.
It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. _ _

Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day. to the Students of the London Hospital : "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the houst. will say to me Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say • thank you very much.' But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew. and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and tills thecup up with water. Now I call it positive cruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become' so powertul in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooaful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement. In reviewing an article in the "Revue Scientifique," the "Minerva,' an Italian Review of Review,remarks that the noted beauty of the women of San Giuliano, in Sicily, is certainly the effect of the custom pre- vailing there in ancient times, when the town on the slopes of Mount Erice was celebrated for its Temple of Venus, of sending for the'most beautiful women of Greece to be the priestesses. This selec- tion of a whole feminine poOtilation continued for a long time, and led rterthe inherited beauty of the modern population.

Some time ago we-drew attention to an address that was presented to the Marquis of Lorne by the Presbyterian General Assembly in Canada in 1883. The address was up to a few days ago exhibited in the window of a second-hand dealer at Ottawa,and marked " For sale." Since then the Marquis has cabled the Chief al: Dominion :Police at Ottawa to secure the address at all hazards,mna.the.result has been that the Chief has seized the addrefis and carried it off without paying for it, and now the second-hand &tier threatens legal proceedings.

The swindler's paan was to get what he could from his victims for his pretended orders of the Lion and Sun of Persia. One trades- man who had made mocney and was arrxious to make afigure in society with a bit of colourel rib- bon in his button-hole, actually concluded a bargain by which he was to have the distinction for the valuable consideration otone arvel of cider.

When Mr. Allen, the representative of a big pub- liqh iug,firm (Longmans), was in Sydney, Premier Parkes, profuse in his attentions and hospitality to the man, asked for a,candid opinion of his poems —how many copies would sell in London/ 'The opinion was candidly given." I think," said the ex- pert, " that you mightexpect five copies to be sold. I mention five because that was the number that was sold of some poems of—er—about the same sort." The "Sydney 'Bulletin" (which is not a friend of Sir Henry Parkes) is responsible for thie story.

The announcement in the "Court Circular "• of the accident to,.Prince.Christian wail° guardedly worded that some of the 'London paperconerloOked its seriousness. It is difficult to gain any detail; of the unfortunate -affair, hut there islittle doubt that the Prince was struck in one eye by a shot from the gun of the Duke of 'Connaught, whether a ricochet, or not is not known. Shots seem to have an unfortunate affinity for the eyes, but the present occurrence is not so sad as that when the late Pro- fessor Fawcett was struck by only two pellets from a gun of his father, one of Which struck the ball of each eye and caused total and irremediable blind- less.

Our German royalties are rapidly beeeming.Ang- licised. The unfortunate accident to Prince Christian is made the occasion of his translation. Thus says the " Times " :—"The Prince has been for twenty- five years so thoroughly identified with English life—especially with its sports and pastimes—that he has come to be regarded as altogether an En- glishman." Perhaps he fias.but only by the toadies and eqcoph ants who are willing to write any mis- representation that they think will be agreeable at Court. We are sorry for Prince Christian's misfor- tune. The loss of an eye is serious for any man,and had the Prince been a workinirman it might have gravely affected his ability to earn a livelihood. But H.R.H.,remains, like the rest of the Royal Family; GeOan, free from any suspicion of English blood.,

The new factory Act came into operation on New Year's Day; and a notice calling attention to the changes in,che'law has been sent to the occupiers ef all factories. These changes are nat so great as the Liberals endeavoured to make them, but still they will add greatly tothe factory inventors' duties, who are already overworked, and unless their num- ber is increased it is impossible that they can en- force the provisions of the new Act. Perhaps the most important provision is that which compels manufacturers to supply the factory inspector with a list of all their out workers, over whom he has now no control. The middleman, or sweater, mist also give the names and addresses ot his victims.

The Government declined to keep its pledge to the Berlin Conference with regard to Child !show, FO that we are still behind other tndrestrial countries and suffer the reproach of allowing our children to work in factories at the age of eleven. This provi- sion, which raises the age from ten to eleven—a slight concession granted by the Government—does not come into operation until after January,lB93, so that it is not of present interest. After Friday it• will be illegal for woman to resume woilc till Our weeks after childbirth. All bakehouses where mechanical power is employed are brought under the new Act. These are the main changes in the new law.

M. Rubinstein has rosolved to decline the munific- ent offer made to him for a farewell recii al tour in , the United Stated, as he has determined not to play the pianoforte in public any more. This refusal was unexpected, for the terms (X5OO per concert, or M.OOO for three months' work)might have tempted even M. Rubinstein. He also declined to give an evening to the Quartet Society of Milan, in which city he has recently been staying. )3ut he accepted an invitation to a-dinner at a Milan hotel, offered by Verdi, and afterwards, before a brilliant tom- patty. which included Boito and Piatti, he sat down at the pianoforte and played for two hours various pieces by Chopin, Mozart, Schumann, and himself.

A ilelsingfors Correspondent writes :—A reform which removes one of the most shocking practices of the Dark Ages has just been brought about through a circular sent to all the Governors in Fin- land, declaring the auction of paupers and lunatics to be,illegal. Up till now parishes have not had asylums and workhouses for the sick and the -aged, but everyone who has from one reason or other had to live on the pariah, has once in every year been sold at auction, and given to the bidder who has offPred the lowest tender. It is strange that, so far as I have seen, no one here whom I have met, nor any newspap.lr that I have seen, has taken the slightest notice of the Ukase, though it is such an in tares ti n;; one.

"WRY HE NEVER LOOKED BEHIND HIM."

"After this I never looked hehinel,lne." This is a very common expression. What do people mean by it? Lot's wife looked behind 'her and was changed into a pillar of salt. A locomitive driver in America looked behind him one day laft summer, and so didn't see an open drawbridge in front of him. Hence a wreck and great lose of life. A mania London failed to look behind him, and was run down by a hansom. What shall we do as a rule ? Look behind us or not? We introduce a man who says he never looked behind him—after a certain time. How are we to take his mean- ing? Why, by letting him explain 'lt. He goes on to say that in one day in February, 1890, he was suddenly seized with dizziness and pain in his head. Like all healthy people, under similar circum- stances, he didn't know what to make of it. He says he felt strange and queer, he shivered as though the weather had suddenly turned cold, and then flushed with the heat as though it had turned hot again. What ailed him? His doctor said he was attacked with influenza, and ordered him to bed. He wentto bed. A few days later the fever left him, but the illness did not. It merely assumed another forms. His tongue 13oked like a piece of brown leather, and his skin and the whites of his eyes became yellow, like old parehtnent. We must all eat to live, but when this man tried to eat, the food went against him, and after he had swallowed it by main force, it caused such pain in the chest, side, and stomach that he wished he had let it alone. Then his heart began to palpitate, and he says he felt low, languid, and tired. He bad what be calls a sinking feeling at the pit of the stomach and &craving which nothing satisfied. Being unable to take any but liquid food he grew so weak that he was barely able to walk. Then his heart troubled him once more, and to quote his own words, "As eat is .ay chair IcoiildJhear my heart thumping as if somebody ems pounding mean the back." This showed that the heart had too much work on hand and was struggling under it like a horse trying to carry two men. "I got very little sleep at night." he says, " and would lie awake for hours tossing about on the bed." This sort of thing is very wearing, and we are:not surprised to learn that he lost flesh until little was left of hint but skin and bone. " My cheeks," he • says, " sank in until they were almost drawn together, and people shook their heads and predicted that my time in this world was nearly up. Still I had all confi- dence in my physician and kept on taking his medicine. ' From first to last I took some forty or fifty bottles of it

(of all kinds) without benat. "Finally one day the doctor sounded my lungs and asked me if any of our family died of consumption. He said that the heart palpitation was caused by dyspepsia. Then he said I had better take further advice ; he could do no more for me. This was after nine months of his treatment. I gave up all hopes of getting better, and, indeed, no one expected me to. "It was now winter again, December, 1890. One day I found a little book or pamphlet in the house, that I had never seen before. It was about a medicine called Mother Seigel's Syrup, and described a case like mine having been cured by it. Without going into all my hopes and fears on the point, it is enough to say that I got a bottle from Mr. Kirkman, Chemist, Ellerby Lane. I took the contents of that bottle and certainly felt a little better. I took a second and began to eat sslid food, which agreed with me. " After this I never taek,f4.behind me, though my re- covery was a work of time,for I was very much reduced: I stuck to the medicine, and with good reason, and at last got back to my work, strong and well, and have re- lmained so ever since. Whenl went back to the works the foreman and others gathered round me and asked what had wrought the wonderful change. I answered, "Mother Seigel's Syrup had wrought it." When I said! wished to start work they told me I must first be examined by a doctor. The doctor said I was fit for work and I went to work the next morning and have never lost a minute since. "I wish others to know what Seigel's Syrup has done for me, and I give the proprietors permission to publish this brief account of my case. lam a cloth presser by trade and have worked at Messrs. Hepworth & Sons, Clay Pit Lane, for four years." Harvey Askew, 2, Black Timber Place, Ellerby Lane, Leeds. The doctor was right in saying that the apparent heart trouble in Mr. Aske w's case arose from dyspepsia, for dyspepsia was his only ailment. And if lie had used Mother Seigel's syrup in February,lB9o, he would have had no tale to tell, for he would have been all right directly. As it is we are glad that after he did try it he had no relapse. He never looked behind him. MORTALITY OF THE HUMAN RICE.

A French medical journal has arrived at the con- clusion that the annual mortality of the entire human race amounts, roughly speaking, to thirty- three millions of persons.' oThis, it is obseried, implies that the average deaths per day are over ninety-one thousand, being at the rate of 3,730 an hour. The notion of sixty.two people dying every minute of he day and -night. all the year round presents our death statistics perhaps in the most lugubrious aspect that is possible. Pursuing his cheerful researches this authority finds that a fourth bf the race die before completing their eighth year, and one-half before the end of the seventeenth year; but the average duration of life is neverthe- less about 38 years. Further he has ascertained that centenarians are so rare that not more than one person in a hundred thousand attains this patri- archal stage. -

• THE LATE SIR JAMES PICTON. visit's TO AEHTON. In our last issue, we gave extracts from the life vg Sir James A. Picton, showing his connection with Warrington. The followin.g passages record his recollections of his visits to Ashton-in-Makerfield. During the time I was at school,l was accustotnect to go over to Ashton to spend my holidays with my' stepmother's family, the Ceets. The house in which, the family lived was rather an imposing looking red brick building in the centre of the village, at; the junction of two roads. The whole establish-, ment was extensive, with its workshops. ware- houses, stabluig, shippon, and raised terrace garden, which had to be reached by a flight of steps. In- ternally, everything was quaint and old-fashioned; scrupulously clean. The front door opened direct into a small parlour, and on one side, between a cosy window seat ad the fireplace, stood a polis'red mahogany bookcase, which was to me like a gift from fairyland. -Some books with which I made myself familiar there will never be forgotten.. Campbell's " Pleasures of Hope," and his glorious lyrics; "The Lady of the Lake," and the other poems of Scott,fpresented scenes of enchantment.. The "Ladies' Magazine" was taken in by the spinster sisters, and in its long series of volumes I de.oured romantic tales, mathematical problems, riedles, conundrums, with a great deal of what was ro doubt rubbish, but to me was intensely interest- ing. There was one book which had a peculiar charm for me,lbut is now almost forgotten—" The Spiritual Quixote, or the adventures of Mr. Geoffry Wildgoose." It is well written, and as I had been brought up at a Methodist chapel, I could enter into the spirit of the hero with a certain amount of sympathy. 'Then there were the out-of-door occu- pations—long rambles across the fields; assisting in the hay harvest; playing with the lads of the neigh- bourhood, who spoke the Lancashire dialect in all its open breadth, the sound of which I have loved ever since. My maternal grandmother lived in a cottage at llaydock, about a mile and a half across the fields, where I occasionally resorted, and more rarely I ex- tended my visits to Warrington, seven miles dis- tant, where I had uncles and relations. En May, 1873, I paid a visit—after many years' atsence—to Ashton-in-Mackerfield, to review the scenes of my early youth. Sleepy as the village had always been, I found considerable changes. The great townfield, intersected by footpaths in every direction, had been rigidly enclosed and ploughed up. The beautiful croft, with its limpid spring of pare water, was converted into building ground and,covered with rubbish, with a staring row of cottages on one side. The trotting brook, which ran across the highway, was little better than a common sewer. Many of the old houses had been pulled down, and their sites and the intervals tilled up with modern buildings. The mansion of the Peets was converted into three or four cottage dwellings. The bell of the church—or Ashton ' chapel ' as it was always called in my youth —indicating divine service about to be performed, I wended my way thither, and found the pew under the gallery where in early boyhood I had sat and mused in boyish meditation, fancy-free, instead of listening to the service. Everything about me looked unchanged; even the tattered lining of the pews was a genuine relic of the past. The service was read to a congre- gation of two women, a child, and myself, and the clergyman made short work of it, nearly one half the prayers being omitted. I could call up in fancy's eye the memories of more than half a cen- tury ago—the stately old maidens; the choleric old gentleman, their father; the pompous parade to church ; the criticisms on the village fashions ; and the good cheer which was the never-failing sequel. The interior of the building seemed scarcely altered from what it was fifty-five years ago. There were the quaint, low-browed oaken galleries ; the roof beams, with the ponderous rings, which I used to gaze at as a child, wondering what they could be intended for; the monuments on the walls; the numerous boards, with lists of the charitable dona- tions to provide (amongst other things) coats and breeches for the old men, and linen smocks —so it is elegantly phrased—for the women; the church- warden's pew, with its mighty staff of office stand- ing up in its place. Gas has been introduced, but the old brazen chandelier, though disused, is still suspended by its chain in the centre of the church. An organ has replaced the bassoons and violoncello :of the olden time, but the veritable board with King David playing the harp on one side, which, on being turned round, indicates the psalm on the other, is still in use.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fornightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, on Wednesday morning. Mr. R. Ileaton presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Davies, Diggle,Aukland, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Kilsall, Shaw, Jolley. Clarke, Dobson, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Suttton (assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master). aud H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools.)
AN APPOINTMENT.

The House Committee recommended that Edith Mary Ward be appointed to play the harmonium at the Church services at the Workhouse at a nominal salary of Li a year, with board and rations in the workhouse. The minutes were adopted.
ABSENT- WITHOLT LEAVE..

The Padg,ate Schools Committee reported that Mrs. Finney, an assistant at the schools, had absented her- sett for several days without leave, and• the Board de- cided to dismiss her and appoint a successor.
THE CHRISTMAS DINNERS.

The Workhouse Master and Superintendent of Padgate Schools both reported that the Christmas dinners at the respective institutions had passed off satisfactorily.—The Clerk said with regard to the dinner at the Workhouse he was glad to say that, he believed for the first time, they had not the slightest complaint to make against any of the inmates for misconduct or anything of that sort. Fie believed that every one who saw the dinner would be pleased with the way the poor people were treated. (Hear, hear.)

THE GOVERNMENT INSPECTOR. The CLEIZIE read a Miter he had received from Mr. Henley, the Local Government Board Inspector, stating that he retired from that office en the 31st Decemberand thinking the Board and the officials for the courtesy they hid -always extended to hint during the period of his official connection with them.
THY. CIIIIRCII-ST. RELI !WINO OFFICES.

With regard to the proposed removal of the offices in Church-street, the Clerk read a letter he had received from Mr. Tauranac on behalf of the managers of Church street National Schools, stating that they would place the schools at the service of tho Board for the purposes of relief for the small sum of 13s. a quarter.—Mr. JOLLEY proposed, and Mr. W. HOUGHTON seconded the adoption of the proposal, which was agreed . 11017011 TON also suggested some slight improvements in the furnish- ing of the office of Mr. Garnett. the relieving officer.— Mr. Dams thought a safe ought to be provided, and Mr. DIGOLE suggested a copying press. These sugges- tions, with the exception of those of Mr. Houghton which Were adopted, were left over for further consider- ation.—The question was also raised as to the rent paid for the cottage in which the relieving officer and Mr. Harrison, the sub-registrar, were accommodated with offices. It was stated that the combined rent was ss. 9d. a week, though the cottage was formerly let at 2s. fid. a week.—Mr. Jso. floccurros : Who is the land- lord ?—Mr. JOLLEY : He is a member of this Board.— It was decided to ask the landlord to make some im- provements to Mr. Garnett's office.

THE CRUELTY TO CHILDREN. The CLERK referred to the recent prosectifiont; for cruelty to children he had conducted on behalf of the Guardians. Ile remarked that neglect o( children often arose from the fact that the mother had never under- stood home comforts or economy in household manage- ment, and was utterly unfitted for the position of wife and ;nether. It seemed to him that in connection with this matter a considerable amount of work of an unofficial character was required. Them were the Board of Guardians, the police, and the new body who were about to appoint an officer, but they were all officials and their methods were somewhat cumbersome. It seemed to him, however, that official interference was not so useful as would be the efforts of people in a better position in life; if they interested themselves in the wretched women he had referred to they might .bring about a different state in many homes which were amongst the worst in the district. This concluded the business of general interest.

div.head: PLUM PUDDING STORIES.
div.p: PLUM PUDDING STORIES.
AN AMBASSADOR'S PLIJII-gUDDING.

When Lord Paget was Ambassador at Constanti- nople, he with the rest of the gentlemen who were in a public,capacity at the same Court, determined on a certain Christmas Day to have each of them a dish dressed after the manner of their respective countries, and Lord Paget, •for the honour of Eng- land, ordered a piece of 'roast beef and a plum- pudding. The beef was easily cooked, but the Court cooks not knowing how to make a plum- pudding, be gave thenua recipe—so many eggs, so much milk, so much flour, and a given quantity of raisins, to beaten up together and boiled for three hours in five gallons of 'water. When dinner was ' served up first came the French Ambassador's dish, then that of the Spanish Ambassador, and next two fellows bearing a tremendous pan, and brawling, "Make room for the English Ambassador's dish !" " Dear me ! dear me In exclaimed his Lordship, " I forgot the bag, and these stupid scoundrels have boiled it without onei-and in five gallons of water, ' too. It will be good /plum broth, however !" TOM MOOD-1S PLUM PUDDING.

'When the genial author of the "Bong of the shirt" resided, on the Continent, a German lieutenant dined with him one Christmas Day, and confaised liking for the plum-pudding served in honour of the day and in conformity with English custom. Whereupon Mrs. Hood promised to make him one, and td send it on to this quarters. Mood threatened to play some practical joke upon it,to put in buVets, tenpextny nails, or something of that sort. 'Mrs. Hood, therefore, watched over the manufacture of the pudding and saw it into the pot without any accident Retiring to rest early, she requested the servant to put it into the drawingrroom, thinking that there it wotqii be out of her husband's way. But Hood unfortimately happened to be writing in that room when the servant placed the pudding smoking under his very nose. The spirit of mis- chief was irresistible. He procured some skewers —these be cut of extorter length than the diameter ,of the pudding and then thrust them through in various directions, carefully retying the pudding afterwards. Next day the pudding was sent tcr the lieutenant, and the recipient of the savoury present came in person to thank Mrs. Hod for it, assuring her that be and his brother officers had enjoyed it immensely. "Did you not think it was well trussed ?" archly inquired the poet. The German confessed that he did. Indeed, he thought it was a new way of making plum-puddings, and gave Mrs. Hood great credit for the woodwork.

div.head: AN UNEQUALLED
div.p: AN UNEQUALLED

- • - In Milton" and Cheadle's "North-West Passage" is a description of a pudding, which gave much in- ward satisfactldn to thoSse who ate it, but which, we fear, would not have been relished, by readers, at home. "Some months before Treemes had kindly presented us with a few currants and raisins where- with to make a Christmas pudding. prom a modest distrust of his own skill, Milton bad hitherto hesi- tated to attempt so high a flight, but encouraged by a series of successes in the sabouty branch of the culinary art and urged by he eager solicita- tions of Cheadle he at length consented to attempt a plum-pudding.' Having discovered some time before that the fruit was rapidly diminishing in quantity in an inexplicable manner, Cheadle had taken the precaution of securing it together with a modicum of flour and-sugar in his strong box. This likewise contained stores of powder, shot, caps, tobacco, soap, and various etceteras. When the materials for the pudding were sought, it was found that :they had escaped from the paper in which they had been enclosed, and were scattered about at the bottom of the pox, mixed with loose shot, caps, fragments of,tobaceo, and .other substances. After taking these out as carefully as possible, the pudding was duly mixed, tied up in the, cloth, after the esta- blished manner, and placed in the pot. Many a time was it taken out and its state examined by point of fork before was at last, after boiling nearly all day, pronounced thoroughly cooked, We had a brace of prairie chickens also, but all interest was centred on the .pudditi,g, No. one who has not been restricted entirely to one species of food for a long time can form any idea of the greedy eyes with which we viewed that plum-pudding. It proved delicious beyond all anticipations, in spite of certain drawbacksin the shape of cars, buckshot, and frag- ments of tobacco,_ which we *!discovered in it. We

ITaiif9ndly hoped to finish it at a sitting, but we were reluctantly compelled to leave a portion un- consumed. We passed the night somewhat restlessly, partly caused, perhaps, by the indigestible ,character of our evening meal, but principally from impatience for the morning to arrive that we might repeat the delights of the previous evening. When day began to break each watched the movements of the other with anxious distru,t, and before it was.fairly light both jumped out of bed at the same moment,learful • he might lose his share ot the -delicious breakfast. Never did schoolboys view with -such sincere regret the disappearance of his last morsel 0 cake as we did when sighing over the last mouthful of that unequalled plum-pudding." A REMARKABLB PUDDING,

Was that which in 1718 one James Austin,' inven- tor of, the'Persian ink powder, caused to be made. Ile was anxieus to give his customers a substantial proof of his gratitude and so he invited them to the Boar's Head to artake of an immense plum- pudding. Dila pudding weighed 1,9001 b. It was put into the copper on Monday, May 12th, at the Red Lion Inn, by the Mint in Southampton, and had to tioi/ 14 days. From thence it had to be brought tq,theSwan Tavern in Fish=stteet Hill, ac- conpanied by a band of musicians playing" What lumps of pudding my .mother gave me One of the Instruments was a drum in proportion, to the pudding, being 181 t. 10in, in diameter, whch was drawn by a device fixed on six asses. Finally, the monster pudding was to be divided ,in St, George's Fielde,but apparently its smell was too nsuch'for the gluttony of the Londoners. The escort was routed, the podding taken 'and devoured, and , the whole ceremony brought to an end before Mr. Aussin had a chance to regale his customers. - AUGHTON PUDDING FEAST.

- In the early part of the present century, Robert and William Lamb carried on an extensive business at Aughton,a small village near Lancaster,as "wand weavers," or what is better known as basket makers, and willows being their staple material, they determined to try an innovation, viz., boiling these willows in order to render them capable of be- ing peeled at other seasons than spring time. For the purpose a large oblong boiler was procured, measuring *bout our feet In length, two in width, and two in depth. and upon its arrival at Aughton, a village wag made the appropriate suggeation,that it would be a capital vessel in which to boil a pudding. The ides struck root, and Mr. William Lamb accordingly had a plum pudding prepared, cooked in the boiler, and distributed amongst his friends and workpeople. This pudding weighed about one ton, and it was the origin of the Pudding Feast which has since been observed at intervals of about 21 years. The lost feast was held on the 17th of July, 1886, and will be memorable in the annals of the little Lancashire village for the large con- .course of people which assembled, over 7,000 being on the field to see the pudding and join in the at- tendant sports. The following description of what took place is taken from T. P. Wood's (Chesterfield) Almanac for 1887 :—"The boiling of the pudding was an undertaking of no small difficulty, and was ac- complished in a special boiler. The ingredients consisted of 100 lb. each of flour and bread crumbs, 1501 b. each suet. currants, raisins, and sugar, 361 b. of candied peel, 900 eggs, 10 gallons of milk, three gallons of rum, salt, &c.—total weight of pudding, 1,23.51 b. It was encased in cloths with a perforated mould formed in two semi-circular portions, linked together on either side and fitted with a central funnel to allow evaporation. This mould was .3ft. 9in. in diameter at the top and 2ft. 91n. deep. The boiling ot the pudding commenced on the Friday preceding the Wednesday of the feast, and on com- pletion it was conveyed in a waggon to the field where the distribution commenced. A dozen young men, stout and strong, could scarcely raise the pud- ding from the ground. When the time arrived for

div.head: RUBINSTEIN ON' " MUSIC AND ITS MASTERS."
div.p: RUBINSTEIN ON' " MUSIC AND ITS MASTERS."

Anton Rubinstein, in a book entitled "Music and its Masters," expresses some opinions about composers old and new. Qf Mozart he says: "Gluck did great things before him, land even opened new paths ; but, compared with Mozart, he is stony. Yes, divine creations I Everything full of light! • I could exclaim for ever Eternal sunshine in music, thy name is Mezart " Speaking of Schubert, Herr Rubinstein compares him in an unflattering manner with women: God created, woman, the most beautiful thing in creation, but full of faults. He did not perfect her, in the conviction that she her- self, with all her charms, would outweigh all that was imperfect ; and so it is with Schubert's com- positions—his Melody makes up for any fault there may be." Of Berlioz he says: "Brilliantly coloured, effective and interesting is all he writes, but all laboured and artificial, neither grand nor beautiful, neither deep nor high; and if you play one of his compositions on the pianoforte, even in a duet, and thus take from it the colour of varied instrumentation, there remains nothing." Here is what he says of Wagner :—" The declara- tion of the infallibility of the Pope has, perhaps, spoiled the Catholic religion for many. If Wagner 'cad composed,published,and carried out his operas, without talking about them in his writings, people would praise, blame, love, or dislike them, as they do every composition; but his declaring himself to be the only true religion arouses oppotition and protest. He has, indeed, composed remarkable things (' Lohengern,' the 'Meistersinger,' and the overture to 'Faust,' especially), but the pretentious- ness and dogmatism of his creations spoil most of them for me. Their want of naturalness and sim- plicity are unsympathetic to me."

The mood of Lady Callerley changed ere long, and she was in tbi'mindito be' charmed with her UW surroundings. " One thing alone Vexed an.d this lired her; husband's frequent', absence., Sir Uncelot bd been an absentee, for so long a perial that now, , when he had returned, there were a hundred matters requiring his attention and needing to be looked into; and what with frequent interviews, with stewards and tenants, and long rides hither and thither to investigate grievances and plan im- provements, his time for monthis to come would, be fully occupied, and his bride be left pretty much to her own devices. It was not a very cheerful Outlook for Silvia, and recognising this, • her hus- ,band suggested that his vent= Mrs. Breamish and, .her boy ,Lance might be inviLé. to' come and stay at Seaton.Callerley. But to this suggestion Lady Callerley save an unhesitating refusal. "No, no, Lancelot, ,I shall be very much amused exploring and arrangbig, and I'd much rather not have that woman—l mean, dear, that she's a total stranger to, met you know,and—and if I can't have, my our sobersidee` Of Ai husband, I'd rather hairs leisure to 'think of 'him while he's away, which I couldn't do if I had to be polite and act hostess to people! Don't you see that, dear ?" Silvia said the last words so prettily, hanging on his arm, and looking up into his 'grave face with such loving, innocent blue eyes, that he entirely forgot to resent her tone about Mrs. Breamish. ' "You sweet little coaxer," he/said, laughingly, "of course you 'must do as you choose. • But .I fear greatly that my fair cousin has not won voiis nears; aim mat is, metnimoi, a Toy, since she Is our nearest neighbour and a kinswoman besides." Silvia made a queer mouth, and wrinkled up her little nose like a spaniel about to bite; but she said nothing more, and Sir Lancelot, giving her a hasty kiss, went down the hall and out at the portico, where his black horse Despair was waiting saddled in readiness for him. Lady Callerley, standing upon the steps, watched him as he rode away. They were a fine pair, horse and rider, with the clear, cold morning light shining upon them. Both had a kind of sombre grandeur of bearing and movement; both gave an impression of might, and gallantry, and gentle breeding; both looked as though by right they belonged to a more stately and earnest age of the world. And to Silvia' Cal- lerley both alike inspired a strange feeling of awe. She wondered, with a thrill of some emotion not wholly unpleasing, if the time would ever come when she would cease to be afraid of her husband.

• She was just at that age when to love is to idolize, and when the sweetest thing in life is her worship. Perhaps also at the age when, to an eager and enthusiastic nature, thrown back upon itself, all its reserves of passion and idealism thwarted, the, failure to attain that love and hero worship proves dangerous in the extreme; . An hour or two was spent very pleasantly ramb- ling over the house, under the guidance of Mrs. Moor, 'the housekeeper. This good woman was delighted to have a mistress at last to whom she mold show, :off and 'expatiate upon the faded grandeurs of Seaton Callerley. With garrulouk eloquence, and that minute attention to triviel. detail so common to those whose lives have been; narrow and circumscribed, did she relate the his- tory and traditions of the family, and Silvia lis- tened to as mush of it as interested her. Through one of the many windows in the picture gallery Mrs. Moor pointed out the original site fixed upon for the building of the house, and told the story of ,the defeat—alike of architect and builders—by supernatural agency. Told how the work accomplished during the course of each suc- cessive day was undone at nightfall;' how walls were thrown down- and levelled to the ground, however strongly built; and how a watch was set with strict orders, to detect and punish the marauders, when until the midnight hour all re- mained peaceful and' undisturbed, at which time quite suddenly and'Withciut• visible hands or any help from material iviorkers, each stone in turn rose gradually from its place, and fell, in a noiseless manner, to the earth. When the process of demo- lition was at an end, the listeners heard a voice , arise from out of the ruins. This voice prophesied the continuance of those nintly measures until the site was altered into another place—the hill upon which the house now stood. • Some subterraneons • dweller—many of whom are well-known to exist in the county, as warders of hidden treasure—is sup- posed to have been offended by an encroachment upon his territory. After he had givezi this sign of displeasure, the attempt at building there was , discontinued. _

As they proceeded' derwn the gallery, one figure in a Puritan dress struck Lady Callerley as having a certain resemblance to her husband. It had a long, finely shaped, oval face, with dark, sombre eyes. _

It was not trial an expressive countenance as that of Sir Lancelot; there was a suspicion of cruelty about the hard well-cut month, and an expression in the aforesaid dark eyes which fasci- nated; even while it repelled, Lady. Callerley ; but there was certainly -e. great likeness between the two faces.

" Who is that ?" Silvia asked, stopping suddenly before the picture, and pointing to it. Mrs. Moor' seemed' inclined to hurry on, but Lady Callerley was persistent. "That! my lady—that is the first Lancelot in the family." _ . _ .

" What ! My husbands narne.sake;and certainly .the ancestor .he most resembles--hough it is not exactly flattering of him to say so, for a more for- bidding-looking old wretch. I never saw! lam quite suro he coulil not have.been a good man !" "Oh, but yes, my lady, indeed he was—perhaps too good in some ways! Colonel Lancelot Cal- lerley Was in high favour as one, of Croniwell's officers and friends, and was accounted zealous and faithful in the doing of the Lord's work. So it is. said, my lady ; though for my own part .1 think some of the work he did might have been better -left alone." ' • • '

"Indeed What. work de you allude to asked Lady Callerley, curiously. . , There was a strange fascination about the por- trait, though the fascination was one Of , dislike, not of 'attraction. She could not withdraw her, eyes, though the longer she looked the more she hated the sight of. Colonel Lancelot Callerley. He would haunt her dreams; she feared. But on the subject of this portrait Mrs. Moor suddenly deve- loped an invincible reticence. • • From details she all at once launched ont into generalities: "Oh, it was nothing. He had been too zealous and probably bigoted, and had punished ,evildoers with too heavy a hand, and brought the family in evil odour in consequence." - Vainly did Lady Callerley demand the individual instances of these said punishments. Mrs. Moor declared that they would never get through the gallery if they spout so much tune over each, per. trait.

For some time after this the housekeeper talked very quickly; piing over a long period of family history in an. incredibly short space of time. Silvia listened with tolerable patience, but her mind began to wander a little to other matters. She wished that there was a horse in the Stable BM could ride, and then she would be able t go &bent with Lancelot! He bad promised to have a mount procured for her, so soon as a suitable and a safe one could be found, since as yet she was not a very experienced rider, though bidding fair to become one in . time. What sort of a steed would this future one prove, she wondered; what colour, and whether it would be tame and docile, or spirited; would it learn to eat a piece of bread from her hand, like Teddy's mare used to do, and what name should she give it? She was sorry Lancelot had given his horse such a horrid name as Despair; and if she called hers Hope, would it -counteract 'the unpleasant effeets of the other? What was Teddy doing just at this minute? Who would he confide all his love affairs to, now he had lost his little sister? If her portrait were to hang here, would Lancelot let her have it taken in the dress she wore at Carleton House, the one that the, Prince told Lady Orinskirk he admired so much, or should she put on more matronly 'attire, and copy Sarah Siddons in her black velvet robes? But no, that would never do, she would look smothered and silly—Would that dear old Sir Jashua deign to' paint her—or was she too insig- nificant?

- All the time these thoughts Were chasing each other in and out Of her frivolous little brain, she still kept half an ear open to the housekeeper's runnm• g comments, and ere long something abnormal and strange in the history abct her attention.

& boy who lived in the city a many years *IA once saw a number of children tormenting a raven, and out of pity he paid them a shilling for the bird, and took it home. The poor thing was yerY much hurt, but he nursed it to health, keeping It in his bedroom, and feeding it himself. As it grew better it objected to leaving him at any time, and chose to perch upon his shoulder whenever be Went anywhere. He taught it to do many curious tricks—play a Sort of game of cat's-cradle, pick out the notes of a tune with its bill on a piano, spell words with letter-blocks, and to talk better and more to the Nat than any parrot. It was quite a delight to him to have this know- ing bird on his shoulder while he was a boy, but as he became a man, of course, he did not wish to be Conspicuous, or to be looked on as an odd and eccentric person, and Sphinx—which was the raven's name—was generally left at home. Often, however, she would escape and follow him, and several times appeared at church, where she Conducted herself in a very correct and serious manner, and said the responses with the congrega- tion, having perched herself too high to be easily ejected, to wit, on the top of the organ. When Alfred, her owner, was employed by a large business firm, she frequently appeared there, and aeon became a great favourite with everybody. On -00 e occasion a drunken porter attacked Alfred violently, but Sphinx, at that moment perched on a chair-back in the office, flew at liim, And so •determinedly pecked at the brute's eyes that he 11 .617 in terror. Otherwise Alfred, being alone, -,2413g, slender and delicate, and the porter a man 131 Six feet four, and stout in proportion, would have had a very poor chance of escaping injury. In fact, Sphinx became so well known on the road between his master's house and place of basis boss that he often perched unmolested on the roof Of a stage which went that way, and got off at the Proper street, like any other passenger.

I_Orle day, exactly how or why I do not know, it ,rnarae Alfred's duty to take a large sum of money 'rota one point to another, and in doing so to cross 11. lonely marshy spot, lying. I believe, where a queer Egyptian building called the Tombs now stands, and greatly feared after nightfall Alfred 'Carried a pistol, but he was, as we have said, small Id slight, and when in the middle of the marsh 7,43 Was attacked by tkree men he was powerless '"e was bound and gagged, and as they led him 'away the men threw a cloak over him. He could ot call out for help, and the constable who was Pasa, ed by the group thought the young man in the wcioak intoxicated. ,„ Only one living knew what had happened cPhinx, who had followed him, as she often did 'Without his knowledge, flew several times into the S faces, and only left them at the door into 'Which they pushed him, cursing the black bird, who seemed to them demoniac. Once within the house, they dragged him to a rl.crn, in which was only one high window, and tied ra to a ring in the floor. The poor boy, who was distracted with helpless 3:314e17, begged them to tell him why, since they could have taken the money without taking him, they had not done so. One of them coolly replied from ehind his mask that they did it in order that he Should be suspected of the theft. " While they search for you, we can get away to tarope," he said. "Murder is dangerous. We shan't Kill you. Some one will feed you every day. Mean- While, as this has been a private mad-house, you will c.o nothing by making a noise, even if it is heard. Madman shrieked in one of these rooms ten years before he died." Left to himself the poor boy almost lost his own senses. The grief of his parents would be terrible; and that his employers should think him dishonest was ranch in itself; and he implored his persecutors to set him free. They only laughed at him,

,• They left him alone. Shortly after, a man brought aim bread and cheese, and some beer, and unbind- ing his right hand, held a pistol to his temple %thile he swallowed some of the food ; rebind- ing him when he declared that he could eat no rnore. Left to himself, he had relapsed into maddening tnisery, when a low caw fell on his ear, and looking tIP, he saw in the patch of moenlight that fell upon the wall through the window high above his head, the shadow of a bird. broken pane, He looked up. The bird had entered through a and stood on the window-sill. A thrill of hope entered his soul. He called and the winged creature dropped She"g," the air toward him. It was his raven. snowed every sign of affection and it corn- zoned, ,hina to have her nestle against his neck as he sank to sleep. b He talked to her as though she had been a human •heihg, and she repeated her cry of: "Poor Alfred! -veer Alfred!" piteously, and that other with which she used to greet his coming :" Alfred's here! Here's Nfred 1" but with the unlocking of the door she uew away, perched on the window-sill and finally vanished. ..I,Bhe went straight to the office where Alfred's aPpearance was just discovered, and perched on the desk of the head of the establishment. Ile was a fine old Quaker with quick observation, Iknd when he looked at her, he saw a cut upon her trek and some ruffling of her feathers. The bird had an adventure of some sort. She was Je.nabling, and seemed to desire him to do some- lit lg. Finally she flew to a table, and took from tt,,Lus hat. It was a trick Alfred had taught her. paett he put it on his head, she hopped to the and hopped on, looking back, saying, "follow as plainly as a dog does. wThe old Quaker gentleman obeyed, and the bird hiln through the public streets, until she reachod ; "3w, building that sat far back in what once was a 'tafclera, now a wilderness of sunflowers and other bil-k'ung. coarse weeds. Up the path of this deserted TIT; ce she hopped, passing a cistern full of ill-smel- • water and a broken blue pump. Boards were across the porch. It had the air of an empty but Sphinx, flying up to the sill of a queer • te Window, with a broken sash, looked down and amed in heart-rending tones: 4' Poor Alfred! Here's Alfred. Po-o-o-o-r Alfred! ep's Alfred," until the street rang. leastere was not, the old gentleman used to say, the doubt in his mind as to the fact that Alfred bo" in the building. div.head: A. KRISMUS DREEAM.
div.p: A. KRISMUS DREEAM.

Last Krismus Day aw geet to bed, Wi' devd quare buzzins mi yed, But not vi booze, fez don't yo see, Aw didn't venter" barley bree." It wuzn't mutton, beef, er ham, Ner goose, ner prato pie, ner lamb ; It wern't plum puddin' ner mincepie, But sure aw thowt it wur" good-bye ! " Aw bed a dreeam,so bad, belike, It welly squeez't me to a skrike ! An' wen aw tried i' bed to sbeawt, It jerkt mi so, aw tumblet eawt ! Aw nowt eawr Volunteers ;nom, An' did ther Rogue's March aw reaund th' room; Wi baynits fixt, and guns full cock, No wunder that aw geet a shock. One big 7-footer marcht th' front, To see they didn't ' do a shunt:' He browt um to so close a range, Aw rayther fancied it wur Strange! Ther gizzerts aw went pit-a-pat, An' sum lied getten a cowd swat; Wile sum wur lookin' rayther blue,' An cossin' wot they hed to do. Well, on they marcht, reet reaund mi cot— (They wur a freetent lookin' lot !) Wen, aw at oncet, ther Boss cried " Halt ! ' Make ready fer a grand assault ! Send him to Davy Jones's locker,— This do' accordin' unto Cocker"— An' wen you've brokken th' pris'ner's skull, Quick march, each hero to the Bull.' There yo' shall raise yore spirits up, At my expense, wi'th' cheerin' cup; An' wen yore gory arms yo' greaund, Thank Providence yo're safe an' seaund !" Tho' lookin' rayther wan an' pale, Eaur British Lion wagged his tail, An' roar'd words—nowt cud be grimmer— " Attention ! are yo ready, R*mm*r ! Baz at him if he dares to stir, Fer th' priz'ner munnot get thro' th' dur ; Or we—uz two—ull catch it hot, An' get cashiert upo' th' spot !" But here a din wuz heerd below, Owd Nick wur dancin' heel an' toe; An' wen they seed bis phizog dire, Aw th' Sojers vanish't i' blue fire ! So eended this, my Krismus Dream ; An' th' morrtl is : Don't never scream, If yore i' bed, an' feel a crush, Thro' ovverdoin' it wi' lush. Don't tak' yore " Special " quite so strung, Fer then yore sartin' to go wrung ; An' if yo want to keep yore legs, Wayter it weel.—Yore's, TUM 0' PEGS." Nyowton, God bless o!
ICE ACCIDENTS AT ST. HELENS.
TWO LIVES LOST: NARROW ESCAPES.

A sad ice accident, resulting in the death of two persons, occurred at Parr, St. Helens, on Sunday night. Robert Johnson, 18 years of age, a labourer at Messrs. Pilkington's glassworks, and residing at 112, Parr Stocks-road, and John Woods, eleven years of age, son of John Woods, a labourer, of 114, Parr Stocks-road, were seen skating during the after- noon on a pond in a field behind the row of houses in which they lived. Later they were missed, and on a search being made footprinrs and marks of skates were traced to a bigger sheet of water in the vicinity. Here a large hole in the ice was noticed, and the opinion that both skaters were drowned proved to be correct. Immediately the hole in the ice was discovered an alarm was given, and the police authorities were informed of the circumstances. Some of the colliers residing in the neighbourhood brought from their homes a number of dynamite cartridges—used for blasting purposes in mines —and these were fired on the ice in order to break it, and so facilitate the dragging operations, which were continued until early on Monday morning. Several fires were lit along the sides of the water, and many men worked eagerly in the hope of recovering the bodies. Police Constable Wall was in charge of the operations, and he had a narrow escape. He fell into the water, but got out with some assistance. Shortly before mid- night the body of Johnson was dragged to the side. An affecting scene was witnessed among the crowd of persons who still remained at the water side. The efforts to recover the body of Woods were continued ior several hours without any result. On Mon day morning the pond was again dragged by a neighbour named Thomas Dix, and about eight o'clock he suc- ceeded in finding the body. The sad occurence caused a painful sensation in the district, and the feeling was intensified by a rumour that a relative of one of the de- ceased—a Mrs. Caroline Woods—had suddenly expired on hearing the news. It appears, however, that the Mrs. Woods in question who lived in the locality was not re- lated to the deceased boy. It is stated that she was the inmate of an hospital a few weeks ago, and suffered from heart disease. Since then she had not been medi- cally attended. She was taken seriously ill about three o'clock on Monday morning, and expired about three hours later.

The inquest on the bodies of the two young men was fixed for half-past nine on Wednesday morning, at the Bamford Hotel, before Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner. The jury, the relatives of the deceased men, and wit- nesses, assembled at the time stated, and shortly after- wards the following telegram from the coroner was handed to Police-sergeant Brooks —"Having missed train, cannot possibly come to-day. Rewarn jury and witnesses for to-morrow morning same time. Burial or- ders by next train to Chief Constable. Apologise to jury. —Coroner." The coroner's instructions were carried out by the police-sergeant. The inquiry was held on Thursday forenoon. Evidence was given showing that the pond was unprotected, but it was situated about 250 yards from the nearest highway. A good many people passed the water daily when taking a short cut to and from their work. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dentally drowned," adding a recommendation that the owners should be asked to do away with the pond or fence it off.

-- -- ANOTHER ACCIDENT: NARROW ESCAPES. Following quickly upon the ice accident at Parr, on Sunday night, another accident of a most alarming nature and one which occasioned considerable excitement, oc- curred at St, Ann's. another quarter of the town, on Monday night. During the afternoon a small party of ladies and gentlemen were skating on the sheet of water known as St. Ann's Dam, Miss Riddell, daughter of Mr. John Riddell, contractor for the new intercepting sewer was skating with Mr. Frederick J. Wallbridge, when the young lady tell, and Mr. Wallbridge also went down. The ice immediately gave way, and both were precipitated into the water. Mr. Henry Pilgrim, of Runcorn, who was over on a visit to the Riddells', ran to their help, but the ice gave way under him. The other skaters then endeavoured to rescue their friends, but once more the ice cracked, and three or four other young men were soon strnggling in the water. Great excitement natur- ally prevailed at the serious state of affairs, but fortun- ately help was at hand. Ropes and lengths of wood were obtained, while some of the unlucky individuals clutched the sides of the ice. Happily, at the spot in question the Water was only about sft. deep, or the con- sequences might have been disastrous. All were ultim- ately rescued, but they were very much exhausted, and had to be removed to houses in the vicinity,where they received every attention. The young man, Pilgrim, suffered perhaps, the most, and when dragged from the water became unconscious. Miss Riddell and Mr. Wall- bridge also suffered severely from the effects of the im- mersion. They were subsequently conveyed home in cabs. The parties have since recovered, and it has been a matter of general congratulation that no life was lost.

div.head: EXPLOSION AT DUBLIN CASTLE.
div.p: EXPLOSION AT DUBLIN CASTLE.
SUSPECTED DYNAMITE OUTRAGE.

On Thursday afternoon an explosion occurred in the office of the Finance Division, Dublin Castle. The room is wrecked, and the officials say there is no doubt a dyna- mite outrage has been perpetrated. The Irish Privy Council were to sit in the evening in the room above the wrecked chamber. . _ . _

Mr. Coulihan, the official in the finance-room, had only left shortly before the exnlcsion, and had a narrow escape. The flooring of the room is torn up and th,i furniture destroyed, while those who had entered the room shortly after the explosion state there was a peculiar smell of explosives about the place. A large number of workmen are employed in the wing of the Castle in which the room is situated, but fortunately they were at dinner when the explosion took place. Sir William Kaye, the under-secretary for Ireland, and the Castle detectives were soon on the spot. Several of the Castle people, on it being suggested that the damage was the result of a gas explosion, pointed to the absence of smell and other usual signs of an explosion of gas. The police at once refused permission to the pub- lic to Plater the Castle yard. The carpet in the room was blown into a heap, a large table bodily moved, and several small tables and chairs were smashed to pieces. A high desk was also capsized, and the papers in the office strewn everywhere. Sir Charles Cameron, inspector of explosives, states that an outrage has been perpetrated by means of a large quantity of gunpowder or gun-cotton, and the Chief In- spector has been telegraphed for.
It is officially announced that Sir Robert Morier has been appointed Ambassador at Rome, and Lord Vivian Ambassador at St. Petersburg.

div.head: FATAL FIRE AT CARDIFF.
div.p: FATAL FIRE AT CARDIFF.

At Cardiff, on Sunday morning, a night watchman named Smith, employed at a brewery, was returning home, when he found his house on fire. The premises were entered, lnd Mrs. Smith was found lying in the back room. The body was so badly burnt that on being touched it crumbled to pieces. After the fire was extinguished, Smith's only child, aged three years, was found suffocated in a bedroom. From portions of the paraffin lamp found near the woman's body, it is sup- posed she was about to get her husband's breakfast, when the lamp burst and caused the fatality.

div.head: 'SHIP CANAL
div.p: THE 'SHIP CANAL
ECONOMIES EFFECTED.

The Executive Committee of the Board of Directors of the Ship Canal Company have already effected some large economies in the administration of affairs. Ihe purchase of stores,formerly a matter of private contract, is now made under the system of public tenders. The committee, we are informed, have practically decided to invite tenders for the completion of the greater part of the remaining works.

THE POMONA DOCKS. Owing to the swollen state of the Irwell there has been during the last two or three days a slight increase in the height of the water of the Ship Canal Docks at Pomona. For some weeks past the docks have been slowly filled by a shoot in the dam which separates them from the Irwell, and this process has been practically completed. One of the piles in the dam was removed, and the waters of the river, swollen by the rain, have entered the docks and raised the water about a foot above its ordinary level. No damage of any sort has been done, and with the subsidence of the river during the next day or two the water in the docks will naturally sink to its old level. No other piles have yet been removed, and, save for the fact that the docks are fuller than usual, the position at Pomona is unchanged.

ANOTHER -FLOODING AT THELWALL. Owing to the heavy rain of the past few days, which caused the river to rise to a great height, the water in the Canal at Morris Brook has risen about three feet. After the recent gale, a drain, about thirty feet wide, was cut to form a connection between the Canal and the Mersey, with the object of letting as much of the water as possible run off into the river. Owing to the river rising on Wednesday night, the position of affairs has been reversed, as the water again rushed into the Canal from the river. It is intended to let the water drain off as much as possible, and whatever is left in the cutting will remain there till next spring, when it will be pumped out.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT,
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT,

THIIIISDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. A DBFAULTING APPIZENTICE.-1105. E. Pickton, wheel- wright, Warrington, sued Thos. H. Houghton for £l3 for damage for breach of covenant of apprenticeship by his son Henry. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the plain- tiff and Mr. A. Browne defended. The defendant's son had been bound apprentice to the plaintiff in 1887, and worked until the night before Walking Day. He then left although five months of his period of apprenticeship remained unexpired. Since he left a man had to be em- ployed at £1 a week, this entailing a loss of the sum claimed. A mutual agreement was, however, come to between the parties, whereby the defendant's son con- sented to return to work at an increased wage for five months, the defendant to pay the costs. His Honour agreed to this arrangement and the case was adjourned for six months.

DAMAGING A BlCYCLE.—Herbert S. Haves, a clerk, liv- ing in Dixon-st., sued Samuel H. Jordon, picture dealer and framer ; and W. H. Welsh, manager for the Danish Dairy Company,for LI. for damage done to a pneumatic safety bicycle. Mr. A. Browne defended. On the 23rd October Hayes left the bicycle resting with a pedal against the parapet in Academy-st., in front of Mr. Hampson's house when the defendant came along with a laden hand-cart, and, it was alleged knocked the bicycle down and damaged it. In defence it was stated that the bicycle fell down just before the hand-cart got to it, and, it being impossible to stop, the cart went over it. A verdict against the defendant for 145. *as given. RUNNING OVER A Cow.-4n this case, a jury was empanelled. Elizabeth Houghton, a farmer, at Thelwall was the plaintiff and sued John Marsh, farmer' of Brad- ley Hall, Appleton, for the loss of a cow which had been so injured that it had to be slaughtered. Mr. Longland appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. A. Browne defended. It appeared that on the morning of the 23rd of October a young Isishman, named Sohn Murphy, who is in the employ of the defendant, was driving a cart containing milk cans to Thelwall Station when he ran in amongst the plaintiff's cows under the canal bridge near Thelwall station. One of the cows was knocked down and the cart wheel passing over a leg broke it. The animal had afterwards to be slaughtered the carcass being sold for £2 10s. Many witnesses were called to give evidence as to the negligence or otherwise of Murphy, and also as to the value of the cow. A verdict was ultimately given for the plaintiff for £8 damages. SEASONABLE COMhIMENTS.—Mr. A. Browne, on behalf of the other solicitors and himself, wished his honour and the officials of the Court "A Happy New Year," and he expressed his thanks for the courtesy that was always shown them.—His Honour suitably acknowledged these good wishes.

A fire brake out early on Thursday morning on the large premiser, of Messes. Tebitt Bros., leather merchants, Bermondsey, London, and the buildings, with the con- tents, were totally destroyed. Some adjoining ware- houses were considerably damaged.

div.head: TBE EXAMINER, SA l'Ultht . ~,LNITARY 2, 1892.
div.p: TBE EXAMINER, SA l'Ultht . ~,LNITARY 2, 1892.
RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY! AUTHORITY.- ------ -

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Aaron, Heywood, Lewis, Brandreth, 3. Ashton (clerk) and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

- _ FRODSHAM WATER SCHEME. The minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Committee stated that the Clerk reported that he and the Chairman had seen Mr. C. E. Linaker with reference to the land for the pumping station and that he had promised to see Mr. Higson thereon. They had also seen Mr. Linnell with reference to the land for the reservoir, and he had agreed in lieu of supplying the cottages with water as stipulated for by him to accept such a sum as 2d. per week for each cottage capitalised would produce, and reckoning the land at £2OO per acre, plus the capitalised amount ID land behind the cottages, and he undertook to furnish the Clerk with a plan showing the land he would require behind the cottages and the land which would be left for the reservoir and for which £2OO would have to be paid. The Clerk also reported that he and the Clie;rman had also seen Mr. Timmins as to whether other land equally suitable could be got for a pumping station. The Clerk then read a letter from Mr. C. E. Linaker, who said Mr. Higson declined to take less than £2OO for the site for a pumping station. Mr. Higson would very much prefer the Authority to look for laud elsewhere.—Mr. W. Timmins wrote that there was no objection to an alternative site. After 1 some discussion it was proposed by Mr. Heywood and seconded by Dr. Robinson that a promised offer of £l5O be made to Mr. C. E. Linaker for the land for the pumping station, and the way leave for the water main.l This motion was carried non. con. and it was resolved ac- cordingly. It was also decided that Mr. Linnell's offer be accepted provisionally. INSANITARY PROPERTY AT FRODSHAM AND FIVE CROSSES. The Medical Officer of Health made a report to the Frodsham Committee upon the insanitary condition of eight houses at Five Crosses, two of which were unfit for human habitation. Nine houses in Frodsham lord- ship were also described as in a condition injurious to health. The Medical Officer made various suggestions as to the yards and privies. He further considered it neces- sary that the main sewer should be examined through its entire length, and re-laid for the whole length if found necessary. The Inspector of Nuisances (Mr. Far- rington) was ordered to obtain estimate for reconstruct- ing the present sewer by re-laying the present pipes,and by substituting therefore 9-inch pipes, and that he con- sider the best means to be adopted with respect to the remainder of the report, and take such steps as may be necessary with respect thereto. DDSEASE AT FRODSHAIt. The Medical Officer made a special report to the Frod- sham Parochial Committees of outbreak of typhoid fever, scarlet fever, and diptheria at Frodsham. There was one case of each disease. WATER SUPPLY OF PRESTON O'TII HILL. The Inspector of Nuisances reported that he had received a telegram from Mr. John White,of Warrington,. who stated that the water supply of Preston O'th Hill was being proceeded with. HALTON BROOK SEWERAGE. The Inspector introduced the question of the alleged nuisance at Halton Brook. It was resolved on the motion' of Mr. Aaron that the Inspector be constructed to keep the ditch clean so that it would not become a nuisance.
EXTRAORDINARY ROW AT A FROD- SHAM BEERHOUSE.

At Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday,/rrederick Lloyd, Harry Lowe, James Foster, and Frederick , Darlington, of Frodsham, were summoned by Win. Clarke, landlord of the Whalebone Inn, Netherton, for being quarrelsome, disorderly, and refusing to quit licensed premises ; Foster was also charged with wilful damage, and Darlington with assault. There was a cross summons, in which Darlington charged I Clarke (the landlord), with assault.—Mr. W. H. Churton appeared for the landlord, and Mr. A. Fletcher, North- wich, for the defendants.—Mr. Churton said it appeared , that the defendants, with several other men, went from Frodsham to the house of his client,where tney remained from half-past seven until twenty minutes to ten, when ' they called for half a gallon of beer. The boy took it into the place, and one of the defendants took his hat, and told him to go round and get the money for the drink. This he would not do, and said if they would not pay for their beer they should not have any. He then tcok the beer away. ' They began to use strong expressions, and said they could get beer anywhere for money. Up to that time the complainant had not seen the defendants, but when he heard the row he came upon the scene, and said he would not supply them with beer unless they paid for it. Foster then went to the table and took a couple of glasses and put them into his pocket. These he had never re- turned. He then went to the mantel-piece, took an ornament from it, put it on the table and smashed it to ' atoms. The landlord asked who had done the mischief, and when none of them would answer he put his back I against the door and refused to allow`anyone to go out until he had heard who had done the damage. Darling- ton, thereupon, put his fist into his face and threatened to hit him. Clarke then ordered the men out, and as they refused to go he went to the door and whistled for a policeman. The defendants left the house, but as soon as they found there was no officer about, they returned, and Darlington struck the landlord several blows, giving him a black eye. Frederick Darlington gave evidence, on the cross-sum- ' mons against the landlord for assault, to the effect that Clarke first struck him on the chest. The ornament was accidentally broken.—All the defendants admitted having had several quarts of beer each. They had been to a football match in the afternoon, and Lowe said he was so drunk that he knew of nothing that had occurred. —The four defendants were fined 10s. and costs each for the disorderly conduct. Darlington was fined ss. and costs for assault, and the magistrates dismissed the other cases.

div.head: MR. G-LADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.
div.p: MR. G-LADSTONE'S BIRTHDAY.

Mr. Gladstone completed his eighty-second year on Tuesday, and the anniversary of his birthday was cele- brated at Hawarden by the members of the family resid- ing at the Castle—Mr.Herbert and Mr. Henry Gladstone, the Rev. Harry Drew, and Mrs. Drew. The event, which is always one of rejoicing in the village, was marked by the pealing of the Parish Church bells. Mr. Gladstone has spent his birthday in England for the past few years, the last occasion on which he was absent being the winter of 1888-2, when he celebrated it at Naples. On Tuesday, notwithstanding the right hon. gentleman's absence abroad and the repeated requests of the family for a cessation of correspondence during his holiday, a considerable number of congratulatory letters and tele- grams found their way to Hawarden Castle, although the total showed a great reduction upon former years. Uncertainty existed in the minds of some of the senders of the laudatory missives as to the precise age of Mr. Gladstone. At Biarritz, Mr. Gladstone 'received several compli- mentary visits on his birthday. The municipal author- ities and the members of the British Club offered their congratulations to the right hon. gentleman. On Tuesday evening the birthday was celebrated by a dinner at the Gladstone Club, Manchester. Mr. S. Norbury Williams read a letter from Father M'Fadden, of Gweedore, describing the present condition—which is very deplorable—of his parish and district. Major Sharp-Hume, one of the Liberal candidates for the borough of Stockport, gave an address on the past and future work of Mr. Gladstone. A congratulatory tele- gram was sent to Mr. Gladstone at Biarritz in the name of the Club. WARRINGTON CONGRATULATIONS. At a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Warrington Liberal Association, held on Tuesday even- ing, it was moved by Mr. Thomas Birchall, secondtd by Mr. Thomas Morris, and unanimously resolved, that a letter, in the following terms be forwarded to Mr. Gladstone :—" The members of the Warrington Liberal Association, through their executive, in meeting now assembled, beg to offer you their heartiest congratula- tions on this, your 82nd birthday. They earnestly hone that your life may long be spared, and that in vigorous health you may continue for many years to devote your great abilities to the people's cause, and that you may ere long see the fruition of your untiring efforts on behalf of the Irish nation.—Signed on behalf of the Execu- tive, W. Pierpoint." BANQUET AT CHESTER. The banquet in celebration of Mr. Gladstone's birthday was held at Chester on Tuesday night. Among those present were Baron Halkett (Liberal candidate for Ches- ter) and Baroness Halkett, Mr. Brunner, M.P., Mr. Jas. Tomkinson ‘Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury divi- sion), and Mr. Edward Evans, jun. (president of the Wirral Liberal Association). Mr. Deeley (president of the Liberal Club) took the chair. Baron Halkett, in eulogistic terms, proposed the toast of Mr. Gladstone's health. He spoke of Mr. Gladstone's sympathy with the people and his enthusiasm in his work, and reviewing the position of the Liberal party, expressed the belief that it gave every assurance of victory. The toast was drunk with much enthusiasm. Mr. Edward Evans gave "The House of Commons." Mr. Brunner M.P. in responding, expressed regret that the head of the house of Grosvenor had gone over to the wrong party, after the family had been on the side of progress for many generations. He.clid not wish to say any hard things of their opponents. They could not, however, help noticing with pleasure that their great leader, Mr. Gladstone, never said a word about the member for West Birmingham. (Hear, hear.) There was a story told of a great Englishman who visited an Eastern potentate some generations ago, and, being in- vited to inspect his host's stock of valuable jewels and to help himself, declared, in words that had become pro- verbial, that he wondered at his own moderation. (Laughter.) The Liberals had for years been invited, both publicly and privately, to inspect the great trea- sures of vituperation in the possession of their oppo- nents. The hard words that had been said of Mr. Glad- stone happily did not hurt him one jot. He trusted Chester would return Baron Halkett, for there never was a time when the application of Liberal principles in legis- lation and administration were more needed by the country than in the present day. (Lpud cheers.) Other toasts followed.

THE BUTTER WAR AT ST. HELENS. • The "Daily News " says :—A sort of butter war has been carried on of late by the police in St. Helen's, Lancashire, against the cheesemongers of that town. One dealer who had placaaded her win- dows with the announcement " Fine butter one shilling," declined at first to serve the officer with a sample. She then went so far as to confess that it was not " pure " but " mixed " butter that she was vending. Mixed it certainly appears to have been, for the official analyst has reported that it contained 11 per cent. of water and 50 per cent. of fat other than butter. " Farmers' Stores Creamery, is.." at another shop turned out to be simply mar- garine. Many of the summonses were for exposing the latter article for sale without any label at all The vendors in these cases did not say the commod- ity was butter ; they only left the purchaser to in- fer that it was from its appearance. But this is contrary to law. In most instances it was pleaded that the labels had been " Misplaced ; " but that sort of defence will not do with the St. Helens magistrates. Neither, it appears, will the trick of labelling in letters so small that powerful spectacles are required to read them. The Act, indeed, ex- pressly requires letters of not less than 11 inches long. it is humiliating to find an "ex-Maycr " among the surnm oned. His assistant seems to have treated the affair in a sportive 'vein, for he asked the In- spector four shillings for a pound of the stuff. " What!" exclaimed the Inspector' " do you mean to charge me four shillings for a pound of marga- rine ? ' "I do," replied the bold butterman ; and he did. Fines amounting in the whole to fifty shillings, and costs have since taught him the error of his ways.

div.head: SHIPPING DISASTERS.
div.p: SHIPPING DISASTERS.

The steamer Blackwater, which arrived in Dublin from Liverpool, on Wednesday evening, reported having passed a water-logged vessel, twenty-three miles from Bailey Lighthouse, in a dangerous position. One mast was standing 20 feet above the water, and a quantity of wreckage was passed.

The Clyde steamer histrahull arrived in Waterford on Wednesday, from Glasgow, with the captain and crew of the Dublin brigantine Maggie, which she collided with and sunk ten miles off the Kish lightship, in Dublin Bay. No lives were lost.
