div.head: GENERAL KILLED BY HIS OWN
div.p: A GENERAL KILLED BY HIS OWN
MEN.

--- - SAN ANTONIA, TEXAS, TITURSDAY.—The report is con- firmed that the Mexican General Lorenzo Garcia, has been killed by the troops under his command, who afterwards escaped to Texas, and are now joining Garza, the leader of the revolutionary band, on the frontier. General Garcia was one of the most capable officers in the Mexican army, and had been in active pursuit of Garza.

div.head: 71E.-*-)k-
div.p: FASHIONABLE MARRIAGE AT
DARESBURY. _

On Wednesday, at All Sainte' Church, Daro-autry the marriage was soletnuised of Mr. Richd. Maurice Hugh-Jones, M.A., of Glanmorfa, North Wales, and Miss Kate Susie Whitley, second daughter of the Rev. Thomas Whitley, vicar of Daresbury, Cheshire. The service was fully choral, and the officiating clergy were the Rev. Chancellor Hugh-Jones, rector of Llan- rwst, father of the bridegroom, and the Rev. Canon Howell Evans, vicar of Rhyl. The bridesmaids were the I Misses Bell and Amy Whitley, sisters of the bride ; Miss Amy Greenall, cousin of the bride ; and Miss Gwynedd Hugh-Jones, sister of the bridegroom. The bridegroom's brother, Mr. E. B. Hagh-Jones, acted as best man. For the convenience of friends from North Wales the 1 25 express from :Chester to Manchester called atparesbury. After the ceremony Mrs. Whitley held an "At Home " at the vicarage, and the bride and bridegroom subsequently left for Crewe en route for Torquay.
THE EXTENSION OF ST. HELENS.
TOWN COUNCIL _MEETING.

I A special meeting of the St. Helens Town Coun- cil was held on Wednesday afternoon, to consider the proposed extension of the borough boundaries. The Mayor (Councillor F. R. D. Nuttall) presided, and there were present, Aldermen J. C. Gamble, ' Meßryde, Cook, Mcliechnie, Harrison, Pilkington, ICouncillors E. Johnson (Parr), Leach, Gaskell, Urmson, Brown, Brook, Norman, Leach, McLachlan, E. Johnson (West Sutton), Walsh, Foote, Morgan, Massey, Burchall, Jones, Hatton, Mearns, Hunter, Martin, Forster, Messrs. Jeeves (Town Clerk), and Lee (Chief Clerk.) It appeared from the minutes of the Parliamentary Committee that the committee have recently had under consideration communications from the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority,Colonel D. Gamble, C.B.,and Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, respecting the arrangement for the proposed extension of the borough boundaries. At the last meeting of the committee a deputation attended from the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority, and the points raised in the correspondence were discussed. Mutual concessions were made, and the deputation ulti- mately agreed to advise the Rural Sanitary Authority to withdraw their threatened opposition to the proposals of the Corporation upon the Council agreeing to certain stipulations in regard to the levels of certain roads and questions of sewage disposal.—The Town Clerk reported to the same meeting that he had had a long conversation with the Clerk to the Lancashire County Council as to the proposed extension, and that, among other things, he was informed that, it was the intention of the County Council to ask for the insertion in the provisional order of clauses providing that the whole area of the borough, as enlarged, should be constituted into one township, in order that the inconvenience arising in the matter of assessment, &c., from divided townships might be done away with. The Committee resolved that as such a pro- posal would also have the result of equalising the taxa- tion throughout the borough, and of decreasing the number of rating authorities, the proposal be heartily approved and supported, and that, if practicabje, a further provision be made, that, subject to the compen- sation of existing officers, the Corporation be consti- tuted the overseers of the new township. At the meeting of the Council on Wednesday the town clerk first read the minutes of a meeting of the Parlia- mentary Committee held that day which stated that the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority had agreed to confirm the view taken by the deputation who attended the last meeting of the committee, and not oppose the proposed extension. A letter was received from Messrs. J. 0. and W. Swift, stating that Messrs. Pilkington Brothers were prepared to refrain from op- posing the scheme on the terms offered by the commit- tee, subject to the height of a bridge over the proposed new road being a minimum clear height of 17ft. instead of Mt. The committee resolved that such an alteration be allowed, and the Town-clerk reported that he had had several communications from Colonel Gamble with respect to the proposed extension, and had received a letter stating that, subject to definite arrangements being made for the sewerage of the City Windle end, he was sufficiently satisfied to refrain from opposing the scheme. The committee decided to recommend that the sewage of the City Windle end be dealt with by means of a sewer' to be constructed under the provisions of the St. Helens Improvement Act, run- ning along Cowley Hill-lane, and thence across land to Denton's-green, subject, however, to arrangements being made that the sewers on the said land should be consi- dered by the owners in the same positions as sewers laid in a new street, and that the works on the land be com- menced immediately on the extension being effected,and those in Cowley Hill-lane as soon as the circumstances would permit.—On the suggestion of Councillor Foote, the Council resolved itself into committee to discuss the proposals.—Councillor Mearns asked if the Council could be given any idea as to the probable cost of the pro- posed sewage works.—The Town Clerk explained what- ever the cost might be, the Corporation would be able to recover the cost from the abutting owners of I property to the extent that the land was already built upon. The other portion of the cost would be recovered as the land was built upon.—Alderman Pilkington then moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee. He said that thelLocal Government Board inquiry into the application of the council for an extension of the borough boundary would be held on the 12th January, and, in order that they might be fully prepared for the inquiry that meeting was absolutely necessary. The scheme which the town clerk would have to submit would be practically the same scheme as that passed by the Council in September last. Alterations of very small moment, which did not really affect the scheme, had been agreed to, and he thought they had fully met the requirements of neigh- bouring authorities and persons affected by the scheme. He dealt at considerable length with the communications received from the Prescot Rural Sanitaty Authority, the Eccleston Highway Board, and Colonel Gamble, CB., and said that pro^ision had been made in case of any difficulty arising with the Prescot Rural Sanitary Authority for the matter to be settled by 'the arbitration of the Local Government Board. The question of the Eccleston Waterworks being brought inside or remaining outside of the borough was a com- paratively small matter. In regard to Colonel Gamble and the sewerage of City Windle, he thought the com- mittee had arrived at a very reasonable arrangement. In any case,before very long the Corporation would have had to make a sewer in order to deal with the sewage of City Windle, which had been a very sore question from time to time. By the new arrangement Colonel Gamble would make a new road from Dentons-green to the bottom of Cowley Hill-lane, near the Park, which would be a great public improvement, and would pay for that road and for the sewer there. With regard to the rest of the sewer from the main sewer in Peter-st. to Denton's-green, that would have to be made in any case, and the sooner the better for the property there. The other piece from Cowley Hill-lane to City Windle would be made by the Corporation, and there would not be much return for the expenditure, as there were not many houses upon the road. The Surveyor had estimated that the cost to the Corporation would be about £l,OOO. The committee considered the suggestion of the County Council that the wnole area of the borough should be constituted into one township, so as to bring about an equalisation of the rates, a very good one, and had decided to insert such a proposal in their applica- tion. The whole of the scheme had been thoroughly ' considered by the committee, who had taken a good deal of trouble in regard to it, and he hcped that! very little, if any, opposition would be met with. It was the intention of the Corporation to deal justly and • fairly alike with all parts of the borough, and if the new area was added they would at once proceed with the lighting, sewering, and other necessary arrangements . Alderman T. Cook seconded the adoption of the minutes.—ln answer to questions, the Town Clerk said that, generally speaking, when sewers were constructed under the Public Health Act the cost fell upon the autho- rity carrying out the work, but when sewers were made under the provisions of the St. Helens Improvement Act the Corporation were able to recover part of the cost from the owners of the abutting property. But it should be remembered that whenever a sewer might be made in Cowley Hill-lane the cost would fall greatly upon the Corporation. As the owners of the public park alongside the road they would be liable. —Councillor Foote drew attention to the proposed new bridges across the road as agreed with Messrs. linog-f ton, and expressed a hope that the road would be left such sufficient width as to provide a footpoth —The Town-clerk said the agreement was for thsrorad:toobne left at its present width of 33 seet„counci.lo rates of the Morgan considered that the equalisation of the i borough had been long wanted, and he was glad the Corporation were going in for it. Coun for sewers Hatton asked if 'property owners were only liable of a certain depth. If so, the sewers in Cow- ley Hill-lane would cost a lot to get over the hill from the park.—The Town-clerk said the sewers would. not be constructed over the hill. As already explained, Colonel Gamble would make a new road to Denton's- green across the fields from the foot of the and the sewer would go hill near the Park, along the new road. The hill would thus be avoided.—Councillor Mearns did not oppose the scheme, but considered the sewerage arrangements would prove very expensive. It would be satisfactory if they had some definite idea as to the Cost—The Town-clerk, in answer to other questions, said Colonel Gamble would be in the position of any other property owner accord- ing to the Act of Parliament. In regard to compensa- tion to any existing officers prejudically affected by the extension, the amount to be given would be ascertained on a fixed scale according to the loss sustained.—The minutes were then unanimously passed, and the pro- ceedings terminated.

A list of the New Year honours conferred by the Queen is issued. General Sir F. Roberts, Admiral W. A. Hood, and Sir William Thomson (President of the Royal Society) are made peers, and Sir Walter Barttelot and Mr. A. B. Forwood, members of the Privy Council.

"HAzEn's Annual" for 1892 is to Old Age reusio„. hand, and it is like its predecessors in taking the lead as "a cyclopcedic record of men and topics of the day." Its brief biographies of eminent persons now number nearly 1,000, as many as' 100 having been added during the present year. There are altogether above 3,600 explanatory articles, and they may be said to cover everything that is current of politi- cal, social, biographical, and general interest. The ordinary cyclopcedia is soon out of date in these days of express speed; but Hazell's, issued as it is annually, keeps the reader thoroughly posted in the latest information. Speaking for ourselves, we have not found any work of reference which has proved as handy and as useful. Containing, as it does, over 700 closely printed pages, no one can complain of the price of the bulky volume, which is 3s. 6d. In the preface, the editor remarks that "Social topics have in 1891 almost superseded the ordinary political themes"; and, this being the case, considerable space has been wisely devoted to questions of labour and capital, of education, and of State pensions for aged people. We can com- mend the lengthy article upon the last-named sub- ject to all who are giving atteution to this most important matter. Mr. John Morley, in August last, said "the man or the party who solved the question of preventing a man who has worked hard all his life, maintained his family and has been a good citizen, from going in his old age into the Workhouse will deserve more glory than by winning'hattles on the field." To the Rev. Canon BLAOKLEY belongs the credit of having in 1878 first formulated a scheine,and to Prince Bmckukicor fax having placed a scheme upon the statute book. The Act is known as the German Law ef Insurance against Invalidity and Old Age ; and, as it is now in operation and has excited a great amount of attention, it is desirable that all classes of politicians in this country should be familiar with its main features. Broadly speaking, the scheme may be said to apply to persons whose in- comes are less than two a year. The wage- earners who are required to contribute to the in-j surance fund are divided into four classes, the lowest or poorest being called upon to pay Did. per week for thirty years; and the highest 3V]. per week. A workman earning £4O per year is required to pay 3d. per week, and this entitles him to 3s. lid. per week in old age. It is obvious that 3d. per week would not provide such a pension. As a matter of fact the employer, in every case is required to contribute as much as the workman, and the balance is made up by a local annual contribution of £3 per annum and an Imperial contribution of £2 10s. per annum. It will be observed VIA the plan is admirably devised for lightening the burden by placing it on many shoulders; but it has two obviously weak points ; one is that the pension does not commence until the age of 70 is reached ; and the other is that the pension itself is too small. spill, it is a beginning—it is an immense stride in the right direction, and Prince BISMARCK IS to be hon- oured for having grappled with the question in this practical way whilst other nations have so far contented themselves with discussing it. In this country there is great objection to any- thing in the shape of compulsion in such a mat- ter; but we do not see how the right class can be benefitted in the right way unless compulsion be applied. LOCAL NEWS.

PRESENTATION AT WARRINGTON-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS. On December 22nd, a beautiful writing desk was pre- sented by the teachers und scholars of this school to Miss Irving, who has resigned her appointment as assistant in the senior girls' department. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.

Mr. J. E. Worsley the coroner, held an inquest at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday,on the body of Ephraim Edward Mucklow, aged five years, son of Joseph Muck- low, a navvy, who lives in Stone-street. A fortnight ago in the temporary absence of his mother, the boy overturned a saucepan containing onions and fat which was on the fire, and the contents very badly scalded his head and shoulders. Ile was attended by Dr. McDougall but he died on Wednesday. A verdict of" Accidental death "was returned.

FIOUNIVION TO A RUNCORN SCHOOLMASTER. The "breaking-up" ceremony of the Brunswick-road Wesleyan School, Run6ord, was inada the opportunity of presenting Mr. Wm. Epps, late eertificatei, tlesistant master at the above school (now head master of the Weston Wesleyan School), with three handsomely bound volumes of poems. The books were subscribed for by boys in his late class, and were handed to him on behalf of the subscribers by the Rev. T. Wilkes, superinten- dent Wesleyan minister, Runcorn, and were suitably ac- knowledged by Mr. Eppg. BURNED TO DEATH AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mr. W. T. Hus- band, deputy Coroner, held an inquest on the body of Terence Dunn aged 3i years, soa of Julia Dunn, of 73, Orford-A. Whilst the mother was out charring on the 22nd December the deceased and another boy named Buck attempted to make a fire with paper and a woman named Moran found the deceased in flames. He was badly burned and although at once attended by Dr. McCambridge he died on Thursday night. A verdict of " Accidental Death "was recorded.

div.head: DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY AT _RUNCORN.
div.p: DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY AT _RUNCORN.

Patrick McDonagh was brought before the Runcorn magistrates, on Monday, charged with having, on Christmas Eve, smashed 13 panes of glass and several window sashes of property in Lyon-st., belonging to Mr. Thomas Wright Speakman.—Mr. W. Carroll, agent to Mr. Speakman, proved that the damage amounted to £3 2s. 6d., and George Tonle, jun., deposed to seeing the prisoner smash the windows with a poker. The prisoner, who said he did not remember the occurrence, was fined 105. and costs, £3 13s. 6d., or a month's hard labour.

div.head: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY.

Mr. H. Wade Deacon prssided over the monthly meet- ing of the Library Committee on Wednesday when it was reported that 4,807 books had been issued in the month; showing an increase of 46 in the lending department and 71 in the reference department. The total attendance for the month amounted to 12,672 giv- ing a daily average of 507 against 407 in the correspond- ing period last year. The accommodation in the reading room in connection with the Library has been considei- ably increased. Doubtless the change will be appreciated by all frequenters of the reading room.

PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES TEACHER. On Thursday evening an interesting gathering was held in Waterloo-road School, when the teachers of St. Mary's Sunday school, and the scholars of the Young Men's Select Class, presented Mr. John Beattie with a very handsome walnut writinc, case in recognition of his services as a teacher of the Young Men's Select Class Mr. Beattie has resigned his position in Waterloo-road day school in order to accept a more important appoint- ment under the Halifax School Board, In felicitous terms the Rev. G. H. Garrett, 8.D., presented the gift to Mr. Beattie, eulogising his services to the school.— The Rev. W. Stanton Jones and Mr. C. Bingham also spoke, and Mr. Beattie replied.

VIOLENT ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN CONSTABLE. A respectable-looking young man, named Frederick Goldsmith was charged on remand with being drunk and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. Proctor. It appeared that about half-past eleven on Christmaq night Constables Proctor and Booth saw the prisoner and another man kicking at a opened the door and asked what they wanted, and the prisoner inquired for a person. The marl replied that there was no one ot that name in the place and closed the door,whereupon the prisoner rushed at the door and burst it open. He made use of most obscene and abusive Ilanguage,although the constables repeatedly warned him to go home quietly. When in Speakman-st., P.C. Proctor spoke to him again, when the prisoner struck him in the breast. The constable threw his assailant to (he ground and pulled out his handcuffs, but the prisoner kicked him on the face and the muscle of his arm, and also many times on the legs, which were black with bruises. The prisoner was not secured until the arrival of P.C. Booth.—The prisoner stated that he had no recollec- tion of the assault. He was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and 10s. and costs for the assault; total 30s. His father paid the money,

div.head: FAREWELL TO A WIDNES MiNISTER!
div.p: FAREWELL TO A WIDNES MiNISTER!

_ Last Monday night the Moor Lane Welsh Church held a farewell meeting on the departure of their minis- ter, the Rev. D. Davies to take charge of the Church at Llanharan, Grlamorganlire. Rev. Dr. John Thomas, of Liverpool, who presided, referred to the large measure of success which had attenned the ministry of tha Rev. D. Davies during his stay of eleven years in Widnes. Reference was also made to the faithfulness, the cool judgment, and the wisdom of the rev, gentleman in his connection not only with the church at Widna, but also with the Manchester, Liverpool and District Congrega- tional Union.—A similar testimony was borne to the Rev. D. Davies's services by ministers and deacons repre- senting the various churches and denominations through- ont the district, amongst whom were the Revs. D. John (Manchester), H. M. Hughes, and D. M. Jenkins (Man- chester),Owen Hughes (Weslevan),R. G. Hughes (Simms Cross), J. Jones (Didsbury Wesley,an College), J. A. Jones (Lancashire Independent College), and Messrs. J. Morris (Liverpool), 11. Hughes (Frederick street), E. Thomas, David Jones, and W. Davies (Liverpool). The most important part of the meeting, however, was the presentation of an address (illuminated by Mr. H. Morris), together with a purse containing over £3l, by Messrs. D. Jones and E. Thomas, deacons representing the church, acknowledging the services rendered to the church by Mr. Davies and wishing him God speed in his new sphere of labour.
SUMMONING THE WRONG PERSON AT WIDNES..

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday beio-re—iir. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, William Gibbings, manager of the Liverpool Silver and Copper Company, was summoned for having in his possession for use for trade a pair of scales which were unjust.—Mr. Kilpatrick, inspector of weights and measures, said on the 24th De- cember he visited the works on Widnes Marsh, of which defendant was manager, and he found a large scale beam which was used for silver and copper buyisg and was capable of weighing a ton was 15 ounces against the purchsser. On the weight end of the scale there was a piece of lead weighing 13 ounces, leaving the scale still two ounces against the purchaser. It was against the Act of Parliament to adjust scales by a piece of loose lead. When he examined the scales on the 24th July he was not shown the end of the scale in use on the present occasion.—Mr. Husband argued that It was clear that the weigher had attempted to make the scales right,but he took objection to the summons on the ground that the company should have been summoned and not Mr. Gibbon, who could not be responsible for their acts.—The Bench agreed that the company should be summoned, and dismissed the case.—Mr. Husband also asked that the scales which the inspector had seized should be at once returned.—The inspector said he should require the scales in order to produce them when the case was heard if necessary.—The Bench made no order in this instance, but en the application of Mr. Hu- sband allowed 15s. 6d. costs. div.p: 'f ' • THE EXAMINER, SATURI ) Y, JANUARY 2, 1892.
INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECRABITES.
On Wednesday evening last, the Rev. J. Pulford Williams was initiated a member of " Charity " Tent, No. 1,911, which holds its meetings in St. John's School- room, Runcorn.
THEFT AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Mr. J. Brandretla and Mr. James Hindley, Henry Craig, a stranger, was charged on remand with stealing four brass pedestals, the property of the Manchester ship Canal Company. He was sentenced to a mouths' hard labour.
STAG Mira Trq THE STREETS AT EARLESTOWN.

A novel sight was witnessed in Newton, and afterwards in Earlestown, on Thursday afternoon, when a vi.fig hunt took place in the streets of both place. Shortly before two o'clock a fine stag came bounding up Church•st., Newton, with a pack of hounds in tull cry, and number of huntsmen fol- lowing closo in their wake. Tnrning down Cobden Square it made off across the fields, and again took the road. Speeding along Crow-lane, it got into Edrle-st., and clearing the Landon and North- western Company's boundary wall, it got into Ronayne's coal yard, where it was captured, the huntsmen and hounds arriving on the scene after the capture had been effected. The deer was put upon a cart and after being secured was conveyed to Lord Gerrard's park, at Garswood.
KITCHEN lUNGERS.—GarIand Builders Ironmonger, War riagton.— Advt.
THE REPRESENTATION OF WA.RRINGTON. PROPOSED LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

The officials of the Liberal party in Warrington have had several names before them with a view to selecting a candidate to contest the borough, but they have not hitherto been in a position to place any name before the Liberal Council and the public. A. meeting of the executive committee was, hew- ever, held at the Liberal Club, on Tuesday even- ing, when Mr. W. Pierpoint occupied the chair. There was a'good attendance of members, and,after certain correspondence had been duly considered,it was decided to invite Dr. Houston, QC., of Dublin, te address a general meeting of the Liberal Council which is to held in the Liberal Cluboan Wednesday evening next, with a view to his becoming the can- didate of the party. We have every reason to be- lieve that the proposed candidate will be found acceptable to the Liberals of the town, as he has a splendid record and comes with the highest repute as an experienced and able man. Dr. Houston rendered valuable assistance on be- half of Mr. Scott in the recent contest of North- east Manchester, and it was then felt that he would make an admirable representative for any consti- tuency.which would honour itself by returning him. lie rendered good service, too, at the Hartlepool contest which resulted in the election of Mr. Fur- ness, and the cther evening he addressed a Liberal meeting at Altrincham. Dr. Houston is the son of Mr. Timothy Turner Houston, a merchant of Ddblin and he himself is a native of that city. Ile received his education at Trinity College, and is a Doctor of Laws of the Dublin University. It is worthy of note that his career as an undergraduate was , a distinguished one. He graduated in 1858, taking senior Moderatorship in History, Political Science, and English Literature, and he was, in 1861, in consequence of his high attainments, appointed Professor of Political Economy. A year later he was called to the Irish bar, and by the skill and business aptitude which be displayed he soon obtained a large practise, and in 1882 iecame Queen's Council. Dr. Houston is no half-and-half politician. He is an advanced Liberal of what may be called the philosophical Radical school, and it is a matter of course to say that he is an earnest Home Ruler. He has for some time been actively engaged in promoting the Home Rule movement, especially as a member of the Irish Pro- testant Home Rule Association. It is not for us to forestal the judgment of the Liberal Council, but it is not too much to say that,if they select Dr. Hous- ton on Wednesday next,they will have a candidate of whom they will have every reason to be proud,

div.head: ST. AMBROSE CHURCH. BIBLE CLLSSES, WIDNES,
div.p: ST. AMBROSE CHURCH. BIBLE CLLSSES, WIDNES,

On Thursday night, the men's and women's Bible Classes in connection with the above church held a social meeting at Page-lane Mission-room. About 100 members and friends sat down to a sumptuous tea, which had been prepared by the men's class. The even- ing was devoted to singing.

div.head: TREAT AT WIDNES ACCIDENT HOSPITAL.
div.p: TREAT AT WIDNES ACCIDENT HOSPITAL.

By means of public subscription the patients of this hospital were treated to a capital tea and entertainment on Wednesday evening. A numbor of juvenile ex-patients were also present. Miss Warburton, the matron, and her assistant had suitably decorated the rooms and a very pleasant and enjoyable time was spent. Each patient received a present from a Christmas tree which stood in the convalescent ward. Brief addresses were given by Mr. D. Wright (to whom the credit of the treat is mainly due), Rev. G. H. Garrett and Mr. G. I. Neil. An admir- able programme of music was gone through.

BAPTIST SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES. The annual sale of work in connection with the Deacon- road Baptist Chapel, was held in the schoolroom, on Thursday, the object being to raise money to reduce the debt of £360 on the chapel. The sale was opened at half- past two without any formality. There were two stalls and a Christmas tree. The work stall was under the care of the Misses Pritchard, Miss Bowen, Miss Stanley, and Miss Seddon; refreshment stall, Mrs. Davies and Mrs. Calland ; Christmas tree, Miss Lyons and Miss Welling. In the evening a lecture on phrenology was given by Prof. Charles Davies, who also gave delineations of character. There was only a moderate attendance, and the proceeds amounted to £7 Be. 6d. - .

J. & W. DUTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE commences to-day (Saturday). Sankey-st.—Advt, FUNERAL OF MR. GREEN OF WESTON. The mortal remains of Mr. William Peter Green, of the Royal Oak Hotel, Weston, were interred in Runcorn Cemetery on Tuiesday afternoon. Mr. Green who had been ailing for a long time, succumbed to his maladies on Christmas Day at the comparatively early age of 43 years. Previously to removing to Weston, about two years ago, Mr. Green had occupied the Railway Hotel at Runcorn, and his death is lamented by a large numberof friends to whom he had endeared himself by his genial and kindly disposition. A hearse and four mourning coaches, supplied by Mr. Peter Brereton, formed the funeral procession on Tuesday. In the first coach were Messrs. Thomas Truslove (Warrington), Harry Truslove (Svdenham), Thomas and Harry Green (sons), W. Mellor (Runcorn), and T. Fair (Warrington) ; in the second coach were Messrs. J. W. Lightburn, James Collier, E. Tuckey-Evans (Warrington), J. Bowcock (Warrington), and John Vause (Weston). In the remaining coaches were Messrs. George Shone, W. R. Wass, W. Hankinson, A. Coxhill, H. Collins, P. Green (Warrington), D. I Barnett, William Griffiths. Escorting the hearse were the belrers Messrs. H. Hill, W. Howard, R. Wainwrig,ht and Thomas Ford, itpi, At thq cerneter:,- the bod 7 met by Messrs. A. 14;htburn, Bustard (Liverpool), E. Griffiths arid H. Coward. The burial service was read by the Rev. G. N. DEATH OF_ A. CRIMEAN HERO AT ST. lIELENS.

._. __— Thomas Tighe, 62 years of age,an army pensioner, died very suddenly at his residence, 40 St. Thomas- street, on the morning of Christmas Day. The deceased served for a long number of years in the 38th Foot, and was the owner of several medals and clasps. His service included the Crimean war and the Indian mutiny. For a considerable time past he suffered from bronchitis, and was under medical attendance. On Christmas Eve he sat down- stairs chatting with a man named Toole, and both fell asleep. Toole awoke a few hours later, and found that Tighe had expired sitting in his chair J. & W. DUTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE commences to-day (Saturday). Sankey-st.—Advt. SKATING MATCH AT NEWTON.

Notwithstanding the thaw which set in on Christ- mas night, and has continued ever since, a large number of people assembled at Newton lake on Monday,to witness a skating match between Robert Haselden, alias "Novice," of Earlescown, and James Hill, of Golborne.. The distance was a quarter-of-a- mile,and the stakes were £5 a side. The ice was not at all in good condition, and in addition was most treacherous. The race throughout was one-sided, "Novice" led from the start, and literally walked in winner by 30 yards. When Hill was leaving the ice, it gave way,and he was plunged into the water, but heescaped with a drenching.

From inquiries made at Fiddler's Ferry,it appears that the very satisfactory rate of speed that has previously been referred to is being maintained in connection with the tunneling operations through the be(-1 of the Mersey. During the Christ mas holi- days there has to some extent been a cessation of work, and on Wednesday what is known as the " day gang " were engaged in perfecting certain arrangements regarding the shield. The strata now being dealt with are favourable to the operations ; and progress is being made at the rate of about 511 t. each weeir. Altogethen some 380 ft. have been bored. The total length that will have to be bored is 8051 t. and when completed the tunnel, which will be formed of segmental plates, will be 10ft, in diameter.

OTra-.J.-8. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-it.. Warnntmon.—Advt. • PROPOSED RAILWAY AGREEMENT. A provisional agreement has been come to between the Boards of the Great Northern and Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Companies, subject to the passing of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company's Bill for a new line to London, which provides for the termination of the existing agreements between the two Com- panies, and in lieu thereof for the mutual inter- change of running powers, through rates, station accommodation, and conveyance of through traffic, so as to maintain the integrity of the thorough services of trains between the systems of the two Companies. The arrangement provides the fullest facilities to the public for the interchange of all classes of_ traffic on and over the two railways. Subject to these terms, the opposition of the Great Northern Company to the Bill for the extension of the Manchester, Sheffield and Lincolnshire Railway to London will be abandoned. J. &W. DUTTON'S ANNUAL WINTER SALE COM/11MM to-day (Saturday), Sankey-Bt.---Advt. THE CoNTRST IN TUE ALTRINCITAIt DIVISION. The London correspondent of a Unionist journal writes :—The " Times special correspondent des- cribes the issue in the Altrinchatu Division of Lan- cashire as doubtful. From information which has come into my possession, I should go further than this, and include the seat in the category of those likely to be lost. It is no doubt true that Sir W. C. Brooks, the retiring member, is doing all he. can to promote the candidature of Mr. Coningsby Disraeli; but since he has been before the electors the latter has displayed such a lamentable want of tact and discretion that the prospects of Mr.Leadam, his Gladstonian opponent, have steadily improved. One of Mr. Disraeli'sfirst exploits was to fall out with the Primrose League,vvhich in this part of Che- shire is a very valuable adjunct t 3 the usual elec- tioneering Machinery. His excuse for refusing to loin the league was that he could criticise that body more freely if he was not a member—a declaration not calculated to evoke enthusiasm for his candida- ture among the local knights and dames. GAS RITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrington—Advt. THE PROPOSED DISPOSAL OF THE VERDIN TRUST FUND. It is stated that the trustees of the fund of .E 20,000 given by Mr. Joseph Verdin, for compensat- ing the losses sustained by property owners in Northvvich, Winsford, and district, through subsi- dence, inconsequence of brine pumping, are press- ing forward to divert the sum for the provision of technical schools in the towns named, for gymnasiums, and for the endowment of the Victoria Hospital, Northwich. At a meeting just held it was reported that the trust deed and the Brine-pumping Bill, 1891, had been submitted to counsel named by the Charity Commissioners, and the latter, after its receipt, had intimated their willingness to assist the trustees, and on formal application they would prepare a scheme for the disposal of the fund as desired. A resolution was adopted authorising the necessary application being made, it being stated j that the interest which had accrued on the amount , invested should be awarded to those owners who, for want of means, are unable to put their property in repair, as required by the measure passed, a few months ago. Runcorn Tonic Sol Fa Choir hit the public taste in arranging a performance of Randers "Messiah " on Christmas Day, and the concert will probably become an annual fixture. The largest audience that has assembled at any local concert for some time past was present,and they didnot fail to show their appreciation of the high class tare provided by Mr. klolford. The chorus performed their work in a manner that was highly creditable both to themselves and to the conductor (Mr. Ifolford), and were much enjoyed by the company. The princi- pals also got through their work in a satisfactory manuer ; but the soprano (Miss Ada Lee) carried off the honours of the evening.

Mr. Philip Speakman, C.C., of Mersey Chambers, Runcorn, and 4, Harrington-st.,Liverpool, has taken into partnership his two sons, Thomas Wright and Philip Ernest Speakman, and the business will in future be conducted under the title of Philip Speak- man awl Boas.

At Haydook Park Coursing meeting this week Mr. John Brundrit, of Runcorn, divided the Ashton stakes with Mr. Fawcett, by means of his young greyhound Bessie Raven, which had previously won three courses. Mr. Brundrit's share was £l5 10. This is the first success that has fallen to our towns- man's lot for some years past, and it was a very popular victory amongst the sportsmen present. It is to be hoped that this will only be the beginning of greater and more valuable successes.

Another start is to be made with the 'alteration of Waterloo Bridge. At the meeting of the Board of Commissioners on Thursday next, the Committee having the matter in hand will recommend that the surveyor be instructed to proceed with the re- building of the parapet wall on the canal side of the bridge so as to get the requisite level, and that he obtain tenders for the building of the wall on the west side to a point opposite the sailroom. When the bridge will be finished is a question that apparently can only be answered in the distant fu _

A special commissioner writing to the Times on the political prospects of Lancashire and Cheshire thus refers to Widnes Division " The large majori- ties secured by Mr. Edwards Moss in 1885 and 1886, indicated clearly enough the preponderance of Con- servatism in the Widnes Division: The danger is that the Unionists may over estimate their strength. Mr. H. W. Deacon, the Gladstonian candidate, is working with immense energy, while so far as I can learn very little is being done to counteract the effect of his teachings. This is precisely how seats are lost. It is intructive to know that Mr. Edwards Moss had a majority of over 1,700 in 1885 which was reduced to lees than 800 in 1886. As to the-present register Mr. Frank Gaskell the other day stated that in one district of Widnes alone the Liberals on the last revision had gained more votes than the Tories had in the whole divi- sion. With a popular candidate, who is a man of intellectual calibre,the Liberals are looking forward to the coming contest with bright hopes. and they will leave no stone unturned to secure victory.

With a view to organising a treat to the aged people of Widnes a Committee has heed formed with Superintendent Keighley as chairman, Mr. 11.. Singleton as treasurer, and Mr. F. J. Poole as secre- tary. Collectors have been appointed to obtain eubscriptions,and as there will doubtless be a hearty response, it is expected that the treat Can be given early this month.

div.head: •NEM YEAR'S CELEBRATIONS AT
div.p: •NEM YEAR'S CELEBRATIONS AT
WARRINGTON.

There was the usual observance of New Year's Eve by the holding of watch night services at the various church.e and chapels; and on the same night the annual volunteer ball was held at the Drill Hall. During the night bands of choristers traversed the streets, till far into the morning. The year 1892 opened most favourably in point of weather, for New Year's Day was remarkably bright and mild. The keeping of the whole day as a holi- day seemed to be pretty extensive among the work- ing-men judging from the number to be seen in the streets, and in the afternoon most of the shops and offices were closed. In the morning at tbe Police Court, although the court was opened as usual, thore was only one case down for hearing, but the prosecutor did not make his appearance, therefore there was no business. A football match was to be played on the Wilderspool ground, but in consequence of the field being again flooded they could not take place. The first team journeyed to Wigan to play a team there.

WATCH NIGHT ' SERVICES AT WARRINGTON. At the Parish Church the service was conducted by the Rev. C. E. Jackson, who gave an earnest ad- dress. The Rector, the Rev.F. W. ave a New Years' greeting to the congregation. Willis,He expressed , his satisfaction at seeing so many present,there be- ing a very large attendance, larger than there bad ever been at the church on a similar occasion.—At ' St. Paul's the Rev. M. R.. Young-Hughes, curate, read the prayers, and the Rev. H. V. Pigot, the ' vicar, read one lesson and delivered an ad- dress founded on Acts 24c. 25v. "When I have a convenient season I will call for thee." —At Holy Trinity Church the sermon was preached by the Vicar, the Rev. E. C. Carleton,' there being a good attendance. At the Wesleyan Chapel, Bold-st., the Rev. J. Gunnell conducted the service. Tnere was a good congregation. The rev. gentleman preached from the text, Mark, 13c. 37v. "And what I say unto you I say unto all." After the usual interval for silent prayer during the clos- ing moments of the old year,the well-known hymn "Come let us anew our journey pursue," was sung. The Rev. W. Gunnell then wished the congregation a very bright and prosperous new year, and they dispersed. At the lievvsey-road Wesleyan Chapel the Rev. A. Freeman was the con 'actor of the ser- vice, and at the Primitive Methodist Chapel Legh- st„ the R. W. Thornley, and Messrs. W. Higgin- son and J. Adams delivered addresses. The attend- ance was good. The meeting at Sankey Bridges was 'taken charge of by M. Henry Morgan, of Sheffield, and there was a pretty good congregation. At lVycliffe Church the service was carried out by the pastor, the Rev. .1. Yonze, who preached from the text Malachi, 3c. 6v. " For I am the Lord, I change not ; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed:, There was a fairly good attendance. BUTTERMARKET-ST.REET MISSION RE-UNION. The annual tea and entertainment in connection with the Buttermarket-street Miesion were held in the mission-room yesterday evening. They were both largely attended. The Rev. J. Gunnell presided at the entertainment, and addressed those present. and an address was also delivered by Mr. S. B. Stringer. The following gave songs, recita- tions, &c. :—Miss Pigot, Mr. Fieldhouse, Mr. L. G. Gunson, Miss Booth, of London, and Mr. Pigot's • glee party. The accompanist was Miss J. E. Pigot. The Secretary, Air. I. E. Barlow, read the annual report. This contained the following : The Sunday school had been steadily growing, the number of scholars being 198, an increase of 23 On last year. A Young Men's Bible Class had been formed, and was well attended every Sunday afternoon. The Band of Hope was in a prosperous state, numbering 70 members. A new departure 'had been the establishment of a penny bank, which had 42 members. The proceedings concluded with votes of thanks to the Chairman and those.who had taken part, - - -

div.head: VOLUNTEER BALL.
div.p: VOLUNTEER BALL.

The annual volunteer ball was held at the Drill Hall. on New Year's Eve. Dancing was commenced about 8 o'clock and continued until half-past two in the morning. Captain Gooch was pre- sent and there was a very large attendance. of volunteers, and friends, towards midnight the hall being quite crowded. A splendid selection of music was played by the volunteer band, under the superintendence of Mr. A.rmstrong. Bugle-Major I Kitnaton acted as MX., and the catering was in the hands of Mrs. Earle. The hall was artistioally decorated for the occasion. A few minutes before midnight a large ring was formed, "Auld Lang Syne" was sung, and the new year was ushered in with a lively gallop.

div.head: ST.-PATIL'S DAVCING CLASS.
div.p: ST.-PATIL'S DAVCING CLASS.

A ball in connection with this class was held on New Years' Eve, in the Conservative Club Assembly Room. About 30 couples were present, dancing being kept up with much spirit until 2 15 a.m. The music was supplied by Mr. Walter Bellien.

div.head: FOOTBALL.-WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.
div.p: FOOTBALL.-WARRINGTON v. WIGAN.

- - - - - The run of ill-luck which has attended the efforts of Warrington in their engagements with Wigan during the past three year! Is one of the mysteries which we are not in a position to fathom. For six succes- sive matches have our local team been made to "bite the dust," and although on several occasions we can point to the Warringtonians having a lot the best of the game, the facts have. been against them, and an initial opening being presented 0 the Wiganers, they have never failed to turn the chance to good account. The prospects of breaking the above record were of the rosiest description as when the records came to be reckoned up, the Warrington men could boast of 14 wins, whilst Wigan had but 9. Form, however, does not count for much in the Rugby game, but Warrington were decidedly unfor- tunate in having to face their old rivals without such a player as "Smack" Bate, that player not having recovered from his injury received in the match against Manchester. There was a plentiful supply of Warringtonians at the Wigan enclosure Yesterday afternoon to witness the contest-1n fact it was the largest gate of tile season' The ground suffered by the recent heavy rain, being a trifle holding. Both teams were ap- plauded on making their appearance, and. little time was lest in getting to :work The game opened of a forward nature, and 80 it re-

mained throughout, scrimmage succeeding scrimm- age, and while each goal was assailed in so vigorous a manner, it was remarkable that not even a minor point was scored during the first half. The latter portion of the game was productive of several ex- citing incidents, and although Warrington had a trifle the best of the contest, they were unable to to break through the substantial defence. Four minors were notched by the visitors to two scored by. Wigan, and when the game was a draw. The game was remarkable for the determined play of both sets of forwards, and the whistle sounded "no aide "it was found that praise is due to both teams for the display given.

div.head: NEW YEAR'S DAY AT RUNCORN AND
div.p: NEW YEAR'S DAY AT RUNCORN AND
WIDNES.

1892 was 'ushered in in these twin towns of the 'Mersey by the music of church bells and the screaming of the whistles of the works. Watch night services were held at most of the places of worship,and afterwards the usual handshaking and hearty wishes for a happy New Year were general. Usually New Year's Day is not generally regarded as a heliday in the district, but on the present oc- casion the chemical workers had a nine days' "leave of absence," and the tradesmen, no doubt, finding business " slack," closed their establishments. Both towns had Snore the appearance of Sunday than any other day. Fortunately the day was very fine. The sun shone with almest summer-like brilliancy, and the breezes, if not balmy, were very pleasant and suitable for outdoor enjoyment. There ware no amusements beyond the performances at the theatres, and an odd tea party or tWO.in connection with the places of worship.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meetino, af the Prescot Bard Of Guar- dians was held on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Jas. Burchall presiding. There were also present Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Mr. H. R. d'A. Willis„T.P. Messrs. Tyrer, John- son, Middlehurst, Peover, Kenwright, E. Birchall, mime, Davies, Mercer and A. F. Mann (clerk.)

• RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 653 inmates this week, 673 last week, 614 in the corresponding week last year ; and 89 vagrants had been relieved, against 84 in the corresponding week last year:

THE WIDNES MEDIC&I. OFFICER.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board, in answer to one from the Guardians, stating that the medical officer of North Widnes district had nominated as his deputy a person who did not reside within the district. There was no regulation requiring that a deputy medical officer should reside in the district for which he was to act, though it was obviously very important that the services of a resident should be utilised if practicable. THE MARGARINE QUESTION. —The Local Government Board wrote assenting to the proposal of the Guardians to substitute margarine for butter for the inmates of the workhouse. THE GOVERNMENT 'INSPECTOR'S RETIREMENT. - The Clerk read a letter from Mr. J. J. Henley, Government Poor Law Inspector, stating that his tenure of office would expire on the 31st December, and in bidding fare- well he desired to express to the Guardians and all their officers his deep sense of the coustesy they had extended to him during his official connection with them.—The Guardians instructed the Clerk to forward a suitable reply.—A letter was then read from the Orinskirk Union asking the Guardians if they would join in a movement for presenting Mr. Finley with some recognition of his kindness, courtesy and ability, on behalf of the Unions of Lancashire. It was decided to discuss the matter at a full meeting of the Board.
TEE WIDNES RELIEVING OFEICERS.—Messrs. Wood and Ilampson, relieving officers for Widnes applied for in- creased salaries and applications were referred to the Finance Committee.

THE MASTER AND THE MATRON.—Mr. and Mrs. Hale, master and matron of the Workhouse applied for a testi- monial in support of their application for simil,ir posi- tions in the Brighton Union. The Guardians present spoke highly of the services of the master and matron and decided to give the testimonial asked for. The Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he would move that the salary of Mr. Hale be increased by £5O per annum. This was the principal business.

Miss Maggie Leigh, pupil of Miss K. Rimmer, the School, Wilson Patten-street,lias successfully passed in *Win. playing the Trinity College Examination held in Liverpool in December last.

The two scholarships at the Warrington Grammar School competed for on the 18th December last, have been awarded to John H. Warltiw and John Hampson, pupils of the People's College.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTIVIT/RS. AT STRETTON.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTIVIT/RS. AT STRETTON.

A ball in connection with the Stretton dancing class was held in the schoolroom on Monday even- ing. About thirty couples took part in the dancing. Mr. Howard acted as M.G. The music was supplied by Mr. 11. Stirrup, Warrington. The party broke up about one o'clock, all having enjoyed themselves in a convivial manner. Mrs. Willett provided refreshments.

DEATH Or MR. THOMAS DOMVILLR. The death of Mr. Thomas Doraville, who resided in Marshouse-lane is anhounced. The deceased was formerly a member of the Town Connell, and also one of the firm of Messrs. Short and Doraville, builders, of Church-street. He had at the time of his death been a Freemason for nearly 30 years, and was for many years tyler of the Lodge of Lights. He has left a widow to mourn his loss, but no young , children. _

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL TREITII.
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL TREITII.

The annual treats to the scholars attending Holy Trinity Church Sunday School were given on Tues- , day and Wednesday evenings in the Museum-It. school. The older scholars had their treat, on the first night when about 20 were provided with a re- past served by the teachers. Games and dancing were indulged in on the occasions, and music was contributed by Mrs. McGregor, Miss Haydock, Mr., E. Britnelow. The Rev. E. C. Hi. and Mrs. Carleton and the Rev. E. Glen were among those present.

COMING ENTERTAINMENT. The children's entertainment advertised in our columns to-day with reference to St. Alban's and St. Benedict's Schools promises to be a success. It is only a few weeks ago a similar entertainment was given by St. Mary's school children, and it W 0,9 then acknowledged that the children did remark- ably well. Monday evening's entertainment is on the same lines, and it is stated that no expense has been spared to mount these plays in a first class manner. Mr.Jolin B.Caldwell is a guarantor for the band, and the libretto of the opera is far above the average both in plot and compoaition. -•
PRESR-NTATIONSTO A. LADY RAILWAY MISSIONARY

On Saturday Miss Bolland, who has for some six months acted as agent for the Warrington branch of the Liverpool railway mission, had apresentat ion made to her, subscribed for by the men employed by the London and North Western Railway Company, at Warrington, and others, on the occasion of her severing her connection with the mission. On the previous Thursday Miss Bolland was presented with a'purse of money by the joiners, &c., employed by the Cheshire Lines Committee. The high apprecia- tion of the services rendered by the lady to the local railway men was expressed at each meeting. WESLEYAN MITTITA.I. IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY,

div.head: BOLD-STREIT.
div.p: BOLD-STREIT.

The Christmas social --gathering was held on Mon- day night, when a capital programme was gone through. The following persons rendered excellent service :—Miss Bodle, Miss Pigot, Mr. Fieldhouse, Miss A. loft (violinist), and a glee party under the leadership of Mr. Pigot. Miss J. E. Pigot and Mr. W. H. Payton were the accompanists. The chairman was the Rev. Thomas Ross. At the conclusion of the musical portion refreshments were served, the remainder of the evening being spent in games of various kinds. The meeting terminated at a few minutes to eleven o'clock, all feeling that the time had passed all too quickly. '

div.head: _ WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY..
div.p: _ WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY..

The second concert of this Society,for the season, will be held in the Public Hall, on Tuesday even- ing next. This concert will be distinguished from those in which chorus and orchestra are concerned, in that the orchestra will take:the chief responsi- bility, this being in accordance with lines laid down last year. For the concert for Tuesday even- ing Mons. L. Duloup solo violinist, and Mr. F. W. Reynolds, solo pianist, are engaged, and Madame Clara Samuel), professional vocalist, is to appear. Schubert's unfinished Symphony; and Mendels- sohn's C minor concerto, are the chief items in the programme, so far as the orchestra is concerned. As these works are of an important character, and of absorbing interest, a high class concert may be counted upon. MUTH OF MRIL WILLIAM JEFFERY. We much regret to announce the death of Mrs. William Jeffery, wife of the head manager for Messrs. Rylands Brothers, Limited, which took place at her residence in Church-street, at nine o'clock on IN ew Year's Eve. For upwards of 30 years the deceased had been a sufferer, but during the last

18 months her illness took a much more serious turn and her condition has several times been very crltl-1 Cal. She belonged to an old Warrington family, and was born in Mersey-st., 57 years ago. Mrs. Jeffery had been married 35 years, and had seen four of her children also married within the last ten years. She WAS of a most retiring disposition and very rarely left her own family circle,but she was held in great respect by those who knew her and her ready sym- pathy and unbounded generosity were well-known. Dr. T. Ste' '-ey Smith has been her medical attend- ant since .le waa a young woman, and he has been I most atleutive to his patient. The funeral will take pliCO on Monday next, at the Cemetery, at 3 15 p.m., when the Rev. John Yonge will officiate, BILLIARDS AT TITS CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND BEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND BEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

It, is not often the case that one can both make a good bargain And at the same time promote, to some extent, a useful public object. But people who attend the fortnightly entertaiuments given a.t the gynmasium accomplish both of these feats. They certainly get their " money's worth" in the way of amusement, and at the same time they are helping to swell the funds of an institution which everybody would like to see flourish. Speaking according to my own tastes, a mixture of MUSIC and song and gymnastic exercises .make a very ex- cellent entertainment.

More cruelty to children and more "exemplary" sentences on parents have been added to the records of the Warrington Police Court this week. The only agreeable feature about these cases is the fact that the children have, temporarily, at all events, been rescued from their suffering and degradation by be- ing placed under the charge of the Workhouse offi- cials. No one who has contrasted the appearance of children who have been in the Workhouse a few weeks or months with the appearance of those re- cently taken from the slums and streets of the town can have the slightest doubt that from a physical— and certainly not less from a moral—point of view; the Workhouse is the most wholesome place of the two.

But while pitying and succouring the children it is not advisable to forget the circumstances and trials of the parents. It is very easy to cultivate humanitarian sentiments on a substantial income, but where the income is neither substantial nor regular the finer qualities have not so good a chance of development. It used to be said that every road. leads to Rome; in a similar sense it may now be said that all these cases point to the great social malady--an immense mass of hopeless poverty in the midst of enormous wealth.. As long se men can only earn a starvation wage by a week's work, chil- dren are bound to suffer, especially when, as in this case, the mother takes to drink.

It would be interesting to see a classified list of the parents who neglect and treat their children cruelly. The Rev. Benjamin Waugh has expressed the opinion that cruelty amongst thb working_ classes is due in some measure to materialistic teaching; but my .own impression is that in 39 cases out of 100 it will be found that drink is at-the bottom of it all. It is natural for parents to love their children, but poverty in some cases leads to drinking, and drinking leads to what Shakespeare calls "Nature warring against herself :" hence such cases as have been dealt with in the Police Court. We pray " I,Pad us not into temptation," and yet we thrust temptation upon these weak abandoned creatures by placing a drink shop at every street corner. Shall we ever cease to do evil, and learn to do well?

The Drill Hall is a place that is unusally associ- ated in our minds with ideas of discipline rather than the reverse, but I venture to say that such scene of undiscipledness and disorder wa,, never wit- nessed within its walls as was to be contemplated in that place on the occasion of the Ragged School treat on Saturday afternoon last. It was a scene of higgledy piggledy, harum-scarum, boisterous con- fusion and wild excitement such as is indescribable. Sergeant-Major Burns who was taking part in the very arduous work of supplying the noisy crowd of youngsters with their teas must have felt his military instincts of discipline and precision most rudely outraged as he gazedupon the juvenile humanity before him. have they no such thing as elemen- tary drill instruction at the Ragged School? The absence of tables and seats for the children, arid the sight of them squatting on the froor in all directions, many of them clatnouring at the top of their voices for a renewal of supplies; others as clamourously chasing, rolling, and tumbl- ing about, mixed together in the most promiscuous fashion, and defying all the persevering attempts that were made to reduce them to order was some- thing to be remembered. The din, too, was deafen- ing—it was a perfect Babel of innumerable and in- cessant conflicting sounds. One might have fitly applied to the occasion the lines of (Nana:—

Each, for madness ruled the hour, ' Would prove his own expressive puwer. "Oh, 'twas merry in the hail" indeed, to quote the old song. The children realised that they were out ' for a Christmas merry-making; and they rose to the occasion. Great as was the disorder, it would have beeu difficult to avoid it in the absence of seats and tables ; but how the children could all get served with tea and milk dealt out to them while in such confusion and disarray, puzzles me.

There are some very strange courses of procedure adopted in Warrington at times. The town is a little bit disposed to be bizarre and fossilized in cer- tain respects on occasions—and I think some of our local prosecutions have savoured of this tendency. 'But surely we are not prepared to witness such a thing in this town as a raid upon people and the hauling of them before the magistrates—for what? —the unspeakable offence of being charitable. Yet such is the unedifying spectacle with which, it-ap- pears, we may some day be treated, should the half threat thrown out by Mr. J. C. Sutton, Clerk to the Board of Guardians, reported in Saturday's press be carried out. Mr. Sutton at the Police Court last ' week, referring to the practice of dissolute parents. sending their children out begging, and the compas- sion they excitedamong charitably-disposed people, said mendicancy was encouraged by the almsgiving this compassion induced, adding that the law applied to people who undiscriminatingly gave relief in the way of alms, and said it might become the duty of the Warrington Guardians to prosecute such offen- ders. Now, Ido not pretend to ;ay that the law could not be stretched so as to be thus applied—the law is prolific in surprises, and in the devious mazes of its intricate lore some of the most monstrous en- actments lie hidden. Possibly the number of actions in our daily life by which we render ourselves amenable to prosecution almost equals the number of acts by which, according to the appallingly alar- mist " Lancet," we are constantly exposing ourselves to peril of disease and death. But we are, perhaps happily, ignorant of our danger in both cases, and I have certainly been in woful ignorance of what I was exposing myself to by giving a penny to a beggar in the street. It has usually been the beggar only who has had to keep a look-out for the police- man. But perhaps henceforward both he• and the man who drops a coin into his hat will have to be as watchful for the man in blue as if they were dividing the proceeds of a theft. Fancy a tramp placed in the dock charged with begging wedged in between two tradesmen charged with being his partners in iniquity I Surely we are not coming to this. But, if tile Board of Guardians really do con- template such action as Mr. Sutton suggested, had they not better commence with the Mayor and the Aged Folk's Treat Committee? There would be , nothing like starting well while they were about it.

Councillor fillSeem44 disposed to set up businees las the local mystery man. As far as I can see this is the only explanation for the motion which he in- tends to move at the Town Council next week. It is in the very simplicity and innocence—or appar- ent innocence—of the motion where the mystery comes in. It is simply to the effect that tradesmen who tender to the Corporation shall place their tenders in their own envelopes, and not in envelopes supplied by the Corporation. What does it mean? There is just another possible explanation. Coun- cillor Hill is an economist. Ever since he entered the Council he has shown an earne•it and single- minded zeal in his endeavours to reduce the burdens that fall upon the poor—property owners, especially in regard to the paving of streets. Ile sees that heroic attempts to reduce the rates never succeed.is and he is beginning in a humble way. lie s going first of all to reduce thessc maicecroounotpc y for estea, stationery, another his then he will turn h Fenny in direction. At this rate we may expect $ ceased. has it il lno t. btieletipl ?stint some decades b e kno cakf teedr ocidf, ut ID! ec irnaotre snbiunt represent St. John's Ward.

There are still a few foolhardy people in, the- world, and a sprinkling of them is to be found in Earlestown. Although it was known that the ice on the ponds in tie neighbourhood was rotten and unsafe, several people threw away a chance, and ventured upon the ice even so late as Monday. There were in consequence several immersions, but fortunately for the immersed, nothing serious came of them. "Be wise in time " was • a motto they despised, but I think for their own sakes, they should act up to it, and have sufficient sense to shun rotten ice.
MERLIN.

On Wednesday evening the deacons of the Newton Congregational Ch apel, entertained the choir to sup- per, in the sehoolrcom. There Were 28 present, arld after the meal had been disposed of, those present engaged in carious games and dancing.
