div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A DEALER IN BAD MEAT.

On Monday, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, John Langley, butcher, 33, Pinner's Brow, was charged by Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, with having in his shop for sale, on the 10th ult, 41 pieces of mutton un- sound, and unfit for human food.—Mr. Norman deposed that the pieces weighed about 101bs., and were for sale at 3d. a lb. The defendant said it had gone bad through damp weather, having been left on the board over- night.—Mr. Norman : It had been decomposed for some days.—The defendant was fined 20s. and costs. TICIFT FROM A PAWNS RORER'S.

At the police court on Wednesday morning, Thomas Doyle, labourer, last from Liverpool, Francis Clark, labourer, last from Manchester, and John Lee, labourer last from Eastham, were charged with stealing from the shop of William Leslie, 65, Mersey-street, on Tuesday eveninz, three pairs of trousers, William Leslie said the three men went to the shop, and Doyle engaged him in conversation about a Waterbury watch, which he did not buy. He saw the other two men, who were in the doorway, pulling the trousers off a shelf, and then he saw Doyle with them under his arm. He said a man had pushed them under his arm. He seized Doyle, and a crowd collected outside and they assisted him to detain him till the police came. The other two were subse- quently apprehended.—John Hatton and P.C. Baxendale having given evidence, till prisoners were committed for lt days' imprisonment with hard labour each. MILITARY MOHOCKS. At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday, Thomas Cowley and Thomas Moran, soldiers from Orford Bar- racks, were charged with being drunk and disorderly and wilfully breaking a number of panes in houses in Battersby-lane and Brick-It., the property of Mr. Clarke Inspector Bowen, P.C.'s Corbett and Hollingsworth, and three other witnesses named Hudson, Hall, and Bate, gave evidence in support of the charges. It appeared that the prisoners were drunk and smashing the win- dows with their sticks one after another as they passed, only missing those that had shutters. They were each sent to pristn for a month with hard labour. TURFY BY A TRIM.

At the Borough Magistrates' Court,on Thursday morn- ing, Annie Goodwell, aged 16, an orphan, residing with her uncle and aunt in Wright-st.„ was charged with stealing, by a trick, from Elizabeth Hardman, a little girl, daughter of Thomas Hardman, 17, Lord Nelgon-st. On Wednesday evening the little girl was sent to the Bull's Head for a pint of beer, and the prisoner met her and said her grandmother had told her to bring the beer and she wanted the can and the 20. The child handed her the can and the money, and the prisoner went for the beer,but only got half the quantity of beer' fcr which she paid 11,d. The police were communicated with, and the prisoner was taken into custody.—Her aunt appeared in court, and gave the girl a bad charac- ter.—On the prisoner promising to behave better in future, the Bench merely recorded a conviction against her, and she was allowed to go.
lIINOIt CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Bafore Alderman Burgess (in tho chair) ,and Messrs. R. Garnett, L. Voisey, and J. Geddes. DIIIINKENNESS.—WiIiiam Cunningham was fined for Altlis offence. DRUNKENNESS AND A SSAULT.—ratriCk Fallon was Charged with being drunk and disorderly, and also with having assaulted p.c. Cunliffe, on Thursday night.— Alderman Burgess remarked that that was prisoner's 22nd appearance. He had been sentenced to four months' imprisonment with hard labour by Lord Derby at the Quarter Sessions. He would now be committed for two months.
MONDAY.—Be fore Aldermen Francomb (chairman) and
Sutton.

DRUNK IN CHARGE 0/7-A--iio—¢ SE AND CART.—Thomas Williams, drunk in charge of a horse and cart on Satur- day night, ss. DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—A 97m AppaanaticE.—Jobn Rohan. labourer, 97th appearance, was charged with being drunk anddlserderly in Bridge-street on Saturday night.—Alderman Sutton : Give him another chance; he was only here last month.—He was fined 10s. and costs.—Mary Turner was charged with being drunk and dkorderly, in Mersey-st., on Sunday night. Her husband said she had gone wrong through going among drunken neighbours after her child's burial. He had done all he could to cure her, but it would puzzle a man sometimes to get the drink out of women.—She prom- ii,ed to try to be better in the new year.—The Chief Constable : Are you going to go on drinking till the new year, then ?—The defendant: No.—She was fined 10s. and costs.—Michael Logan, drunk anct disorderly in Bridge-st., on Sunday night, was dismissed on payment of costs. _ _ _

_ Does AT LARGII.—Sarah Heaton, beerhouse-keeper, William-st., for allowing a dog to be at large unmuzzled in Winwick-road, on the 22nd ult.' was discharged on the payment of costs. Aldermag Sutton said the new orders from the authorities made it necessary that these cases should be looked after very carefully.—Anthony Connor, for like offences in Buttermarket-at. and Or- ford-st., 10s.—John Porter was charged with allowing his dog to be at large in Butterrnarket-st., unmuzzled on the 22nd ult. Fined 4s. 6d. costs.—John Wright, in Battersby-lane, on the 23rd ult., fined the costs. OBSTRUCTING THE STREZT.—William Percival, farmer, Rill Cliffe Farm, for allowing his horse and cart to stand longer than necessary in Lyme-st., on the 23rd ult., was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, Ils, in all.—Felix Summers was charged with allowing a quantity of coke to be tipped opposite his shop in Bridge-st., after 9 a.m., on the 23rd ult. The defendant said Bridge Foot, where his shop was,was not Bridge-st. It appeared to him as if it was no street at all.—Alderman Sutton : You might as well save your time. We will take it as a street.—The de- fendant was discharged on payment of costs. AN UNREGISTERED LontuNG-Housz.—Hannah biker, No. 8 bower Ship Yard, was charged with keeping on the 14th ult., a lodging-house without registration.—Mr. Norman said the house was overcrowded, and in a filthy condition, and the winnan was not fit to keep a lodging-house; nor was the neighbourhood a fit one to have such a place in. If she would promise to go to the workhouse he would withdraw the case; and it might be adjourned to see whether she did so.—The case was ad- journed for 14 days to allow her to consider the matter. OFFENsm ournocecs.—flenry Atherton, James Gal- Viii, and Martha Wilkinson for having offensive out- houses on their premises 4,5, and 6 Mill-st., were fined is. each.—Emma Bennett and Elizabeth Burchall, 48 and 50, Eldon-st., charged with like offences,weredismissed. —John Buckley, William Boscow, and William Mason 88, 90, and 92 Church-st., charged with like offences, were fined Is. each.—Bridget Rafferty and John Fallon, Ship Yard, for like offences were finid is. each. • •

- -------- - TIIESDAY.—Before Alderman ,Platt, Messrs. R. Garnett, G. J. Guest, and W. Owen. • DRIINICENNESS.—John Smith,for having been drank in Buttertnarket-It., on the previous night was fined 55. and costs. . A Cr...mix OUT OF EMPLOYMENT.—Edward Wilson, who was chiefly noticeable owing to the large lot of unkempt hair he had on his head, was charged with having travelled from Manchester to Warrington by the London and North-Western Railway on the previous day without having paid for his ticket. A ticket collector from Bank Quay Station said he asked the prisoner for his ticket but he replied that he had not got one, and,further than

that, had no money to pay the fate.—The prisoner, in answer to the Bench, said he was a clerk but had had no work to do for aboutl2 months. He had been attempt- ing to travel from Manchester to Liverpool but " it had not come off." He was fined ss. and the railway fare, the alternative being seven days' imprisonment. INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE.—Thomas Flannery and Mich. Duggan, two young Irish navvies, were charged with having stolen a purse and 155., the property of Michael Towey. It appears that Towey, who is also an Irish labourer,had arrived a stranger in the town on Monday. He knew a person named Duffy,who lives in Stanley-st., and after looking him up, they both adjourned to the Old House-at-Home beerhouse, on Friars-green. At this plare were Flannery and Duggan, along with others,and a considerable quantity of beer seems to have been con- sumed amongst them. According to Towey, when he left the house Flannery,accompanied,it was supposed,by Duggan, followed, and offered to take him to lodgings, but instead of that they took him down a narfow lane, and while one of the men held a hand over his mouth the other took the purse containing the money from within his waistcoat. They then knocked his head against the wall and made off. Information was given to the police, and the two prisoners were arrested. After hearing the case at seine length, the Bench con- sidered the evidence was insufficient for a conviction, and they dismissed it. WEDNFSDAY.—Refore Mr. Councillor_ John Fairclough

(chairman) and Alderman Wright. FRAUDULENT ENLISTMENT.—James Hindley and Henry McGarry; soldiers at Orford Thirracks, were charged with making a false answer on attestation for enlistment that they had not been convicted by a civil power, whereas they had been. They were each sentenced to a month's imprisonment. PURCHASING MILITARY BOOTS FROM A SOLDIER.—Peter Larkin, labourer, 1 Stanley-st., and Martin Hart, labourer, 14 Friars Green, were charged with buying a pair of military boots from a soldier named Gibbon on Monday.—Gibbon deposed to selling the boots while in uniform to the prisoner Hart for 4s. He would be punished by the military authorities for doing so. Lar- kin was not present.—lt was proved, however, that Larkin was concerned in the matter. He was fined DN. and costs and Hart 20s. and COSI& DRUNK.—Louisa Jones, drunk in Dakin's-yard on Tuesday night, Ss. and costs. ASSAULTING HIS MOTTIHR.—John Carroll, labourer, 5, Bakehouse-yard, Latchford, was charged under a war- rant with assaulting his mother, on the Ist of October. The complainant said he threw a knife to her,and knocked her down and used her shamefully. P.C.Barlow said he and P.C. Clough apprehended the prisoner that morn- ing, and lie was very violent, and threatened to do for his mother then. He had been sentenced to 14 days' im- prisonment before for assaulting his mother ; and was now sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment. Tnunsnay.—Before Alderman Sutton (chairman), Coun- cillor James Fairclough, and Captain Ridgeway.

ASSAULT BY A DRUNKEN SAlLOR.—rhomas Galvin, a sailor, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Market Gate on Wednesday night and with assault- ing Thomas Watmough on the same occasion.— D. S. Monaghan and Thomas Watmough proved the charges. Watmough said he was talking to a few friends in the Rose and Crown passage when the defendant came up and naked for a match and used some disgusting language. Witness went up Bridge-street with one of his friends, and the defendant followed them, using bad language all the way, and at Market Gate struck him, and then ran away, running into Sergeant Monaghan's hands.—Alderman Sutton: Into safe hands. —The prisoner, who was reminded that he had been in court 15 times, said Watmough struck him first, but he was sent to jail for a month's hard labour.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. C. Parr (chairman), J. Mar- son, H. Neil& and W. Long. TRANSFER OF LICRNSE.—Mr. Whitlow applied for the transfer of the license of the Red Lion, Preston Brook, to his son. The application was acceded to. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Mitchell, at Whitley on the 18th of May, ss. costs. Frank Millington, at Appleton, on the 16th of December, ss, and costs. CYCLING ON THE FOOTPATIL—Henry White, of Latch- ford, for riding, at Grappanhall, a bicycle on the foot- path, on the 20th of December, was fined ss. including costs.

RIDING WITHOUT RElNS.—Thomas Shaw, of Latchford, was charged with driving a lurry and two horses with- out reins at Little Leigh, on the 18th of December, and fined ss. including costs. DOGS AT LlEGE.—Thomas Baxter, farmer, of Dutton, charged with allowing his dog at large unmuzzled, at Little Leigh, on December lath, was dismissed.—Joseph Simcock, 16, Hill-street, Warrington, was charged with committing a like offence at Grappenhall, on the 6th of December, and fined 53. including cos!'s. 800 WITHOUT LICENSE.—FIenry Booth, farmer. of Antrobus, for keeping a dog without a license, was fined 10s. including costs. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS.—James Pilling, of Mill-st., Warrington, was charged with cruelly treating a horse at Walton Superior, on the 2nd of December.—The de- fendant was driving the horse with a greengrocer's cart, and was flogging it unmercifully for about 150 yards. He was fined 55., the Chairman remarking that if the defendant was convicted again of such an offence he would be severely dealt with, as there was too much of this whipping of horses about the country.—Jonathan Pilling, hawker, of Northwich was charged with cruelly treating a horse near Wilderspool brewery, on the night of the 3rd of December. P.C.s Shatwell and Brew de- posed to the horse being so weak as to fall in the road, and the defendant was trying for an hour to get it up but could not. It was too weak to walk, and groaned very much.—Tho defendant said he did all he could for the horse. He conld not carry it away, and he packed it up with straw and left it where it was.—lnspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said on the 4th Dec., he examined the body of the horse at the knacker's yard, where it had been killed, after lying all night in the road. It had beep suffering from congestion of the lungs, and was in poor condition.—Joseph Pilling was called for the de- fence, and said the horse was subject to fits, which caused it to fall. The horse was only going to Stockton Heath, on the night of the 3rd of December. It was fit to work.—The magistrates, after some private consid- eration, dismissed the case, not being satisfied that the defendant knew the state the horse was in.—John Allen, sen. of Barnton, near Northwich, was charged with cruelty to a horse by causing it to be worked in an unfit state and John Allen, jun., with working it in that state, on the canal bank on the 3rd inst.—lnspector Dowty proved the case. The junior defendant was working the horse by pulling a barge with it, it being excessively lame. the senior defendant was fined 103. and costs, and the junior 3s. 6d. Costs. OBSTRUCTING THE HIGHWAY. Daniel Briggs, of Wilder3pool, was charged with obstructing Runcorn-rd., at Little Leigh, by leaving a brewer's dray thereon from 7 p.m. on the Ist November till 3 p.m. on the following Monday. He was fined 10s. and costs.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. Tnurtsbair.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. H. Wade
Deacon.

A DISORDERLY WOMAN .—Mary Ann Barker was sent- enced to seven days hard labour for being guilty of indecent conduct. DRIINEENNESS.—EIizabeth Bushell, who had been previously convicted 37 times, was fined 7s. 6d. and costs for being drunk. For a like offence Thomas Griffin was fined ss. and costs.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

V Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER.

These clubs met for the first time on Boxing Day, at Wilderspool. The sudden thaw of Friday night, and the covering of the lower ground with hay, had ren dered play practicable, and there would be considerably over 5,000 assembled at the time announced to kick- off—three o'clock. This is the first time that Manchester have figured on the Warrington card, and if we are to judge by the display given, the fixture is likely to prove a "standing dish." Representative teams were placed in the field, and Ashton losing the toss, deputed Turner to kick off, de- fending the river goal. Cross's return was but faint, but his deficiency was fully made up when Mullineux headed the Manchester forwards well within the home qPuaralrat.ne ers .a nTah emaot itesa cwk owr tahs m trying a nta rindneeff feocrt uaabl yr i e tf o periodbr break through, the sure tackling a Heesom and Evans saving the lines. By degrees the oval was worked out of danger, James Bate, Heesom, Jolley, and Knowles all being prominent, and then the former baffled Mullineux beautifully, and running down the open, punted past Carson, only to find Molesworth and Cross possess a finer turn of speed, and negative a brilliant piece of work. Passing by John Bate to Heesom, who was held when becoming dangerous, Webster then tried his hand from a pass by fleesorn, but he stepped into touch five yards from the line. Again Manchester relieved, the cross dribbling having its effect, and Smith was duly applauded for a fine effort. The home forwards rushed the visitors back again, and Turner supplement- ing some useful work by Evans, Molesworth was tackled in close proximity to his goal. Nevins next threw across to Evans, but the pass was defective, and by this means Manchester again eased the pressure. A spell of even play followed at centre, and although the game was carried on in a vigorous spirit, not the least signs of roughness were introduced. Cross and Boscow ex- changed kicks with no distinct advantage to either side, and then a penalty kick to Nevins raised the siege once more. Time after time the oval was worked to the line, with barren results, and Hulse leading the Manchester forwards in fine style, Mullineux took up the movement, but Molesworth and Cross were slow in giving and tak-

div.head: EXAMINER. SATUR Y, JANUARY 2, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATUR Y, JANUARY 2, 1892.

ing a pass, and failed to make the best ot a fine chance. Wincey was next finely tackled by Webster at the home quarter-flag, but Ashton got clear from some loose play, and after changing the venue to the opposite twenty-five, passed to Thorniley for the latter to throw a shade for- ward. A free kick to the visitors was charged by James Bate, and the same player had hard luck a moment later, when Molesworth pulled him up under the posts. Warrington were now penalized, but Jolley soon had the Warringtonians back at their old game, and Carson was severely tested. Some beautiful passing by the two Bates was productive of Evans being safely tackled by Gross, but a rush by Turner and Jolley took the oval over the line, and War- rington confidently claimed a major point. A deaf ear was turned to the appeal,a like result awaiting an effort by Holmes. Webster next punted across, and forced a first minor. A couple of passing movements initiated by the home half-backs had a. futile ending, and when the whistle sounded half-trifle Warrington were still attack- ing, and the score a minor in their favour. On resum- ing. Teare and Ashton charged the kick-off, and a slight spell of exchanges found the game at the river goal. A grand run by Cross was brought to a termination by Boscow. Ashton now led up his men in true style, and Manchester had all their work cut out to save their cita- del. The fast pace at which the game had been carried, on had now an effect on the visitors, for they began to tire dreadfully. Webster repeatedly foiled Wincey in his endeavours to clear,and after James Rate had tricked Parlane, the oval was worked over the line under the posts, Thorniley completing a try amidst ringing chens which were renewed when Heesom converted. This was the turning point of the game, for the play was scarcely out of the Manchester quarters. A fine display between the Bates, Heesom, Evans, and Webster saw the latter being held near the line, and after Moresworth and Wincey had slightly relieved, Evans got clear from the ruck, and running down at a fast pace he ran to Garson, and passing across to hi •3 companions, the effort was pro- ductive of Bandies scoring a fine try near the posts, which Heesom failed to convert. The visitors were now thoroughly defeated, and although Wineey put in a fine run once when Knowles tackled him. Warrington were always masters of the situation, and near the close the score was augmented by a try by Evans, Turner failing at the place. When time was called the Warrington- ians were found to be winners of a grand game by 1 goal, 2 tries, and .3. minor to nil. . _

- Teams :—Manchester R. H. Carson. full-back; G. P. Wincey,A. H. Molesworth,and TI. K. Cross,three-quarter backs ; W. Parlane,and M. Mullineux, half-backs; N. Cameron (captain), J. Tait, H. C. Coghlan, H. J. Mothersill, R. L. Flulsea. H. Smith, A. C. Broadbent, A. Taylor, and C. Jones, forwards. Warrington : J. Boscow, full back; .1. W. Evans, J. Heesom, and H. Webster, three-quarter backs; James T. Bate and John T. Bate, halfbacks; H. Ashton (captain), F. Turner, W. Handles, J. Holmes, J. Knowles, H. Teare,J. Jolley, J. T. Thorniley, and IV. Nevins, forwards. Referee. Mr. J. Mills, Swinton. Touch fudges, Mr. W. H. Bleakley and Mr. W. Povey. STOCKTON HEATH 2ND V. GRAPPENHALL.--Grappen- hall visited Stockton Heath on Monday with a strong teatn,being assisted by several of the Warrington Parish Church and St. Mary's. The home team kicked off, and soon forced the visitors to kick dead. The droo-out was received by Downs, who made a futile attempt at goal. The visitors took play to mid-field, where Barber for the I visitors obtained possession and made tracks for the home line. and was smartly tackled by Downs. Thread- gold and Lawless transferred play to the visitors' quart- ers, where Cross had a shot at goal, but the oval failed to rise. Half-time arrived with Stockton Heath 4 minors to ail. On resuming, the home forwards broke away to the visitors' lines and Twigs gainld a try, no goal resulting. The drop-out found the homesters again pressing, and Ashurst scored another try,Glover landing a goal. Nothing further being scored, Stockton Heath ran out victors by 1 goal, 1 try, el minors to nil.

gaining a try between the post, Crompton improved the score by kicking a neat goal. Resuming from centre, ' Buckett sent the leather to Houghton, who fumbled a bit, but a moment later showed all his old cleverness in disposing of the leather whilst surrounded ,though follow- ing the return the Cheshire full-back got his side penal- ised for lying on the leather. Nothing came of the kick,and some lively exchanges between the backs ended in Cheshire's favour, but a moment later Jones had his Kick ' charged down, and the ball was carried over the line, and a minor to Cumberland was the result. Following this, a fine attack was made on the home citadel, Sand- with running well, though his passing was rather wild. Still keeping up a strong attack, Cumberland at length got through the Cheshire defence, Davidson scoring at the corner. Buckett made a poor attempt at the place. A pretty bit of play was witnessed between Hodgkinson and Johnson, which was instrumental in forcing the home team on the defensive, and while the game was in the Cheshire " 25 " the ball was kicked to Lamonby,who with a beautiful coolness ran towards the goal, and splendidly dropped the ball over the bar. This put the visitors ahead by six points to live, and at this stage the intervalwas announced. Following the kick off,the visi- tors got into their opponents' quarter, where they com- menced attacking in clever style. Hodgkinson dropped at goal without success, though it deserved it. A little laxity on Cheshire's part was seized by the active Hodg- kinson, who bounded away, and was going great runs when Jones overtook him. The game was getting ex- citing, and a little humour was infused into the bustling business when Houghton had his jersey torn in rags, and while in this semi-barbalic state he was continually pep- pered at by the opposing backs. A pretty exhibition of clever dribbling by Davidson and Buckett, carried kostilities into- the Cheshire quarter, Houghton saving finely, and Mutchie, Cuthertson,and Hodgkinson further improved the advantage gained. While in the vicinity of the home goal Davidson got possession, and giving Buckett a well-timed pass the latter was enabled to get over the line without any difficulty, scoring a try, which he afterwards failed to improve. After smart tactics by .the visitors, which were repulsed on two occasions- by the powerful punting of Hough- ton the Cheshire forwards rushed up and carried the leather near the Cumberland goal, where some severe struggling took place, when Riley passed out to Cromp- tons who, with a positive try at his mercy, very ques- tionably preferred to drop at goal. The attempt was eminently successful, and the cheers which greeted the feat showed the feeling of the spectators. Then Cromp- ton dropped at goal and missed his object, and just when time was about up Davies got possession and dashed over the line. scoring a try, which Crompton tried to convert without getting his deserts. The signal for ces- sation was then given, and Cheshire retired with a victory the score reading—Cheshire, 2 goals (1 dropped), 1 try, (11 points) ; Cumberland, 1 goal, (dropped), 2 tries (8 points.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at the Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday under the presidency of Mr, Mclntyre. Present the Rev. .7. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., S. Taylor, E. Aaron, Lewis, Lea, Baxter, Heywood, Edwards, Brandreth, J. Ashton (clerk)', and G. Aehton (deputy clerk).

div.head: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN v. BRADFORD.

The Bradford team came very near coming an unexpected cropper on Saturday, when Runcorn paid them their annnal visit. The Cheshire men held a strong lead the greater portion of the game, but ultimately Bradford notched a major point in the last few minutes, and managed to make a draw. A liberal application of salt and hot water had rendered the ground, if anything a trifle too soft, and without the thaw which set in on Saturday the turf would have been quite fit for play. Rain fell in the afternoon, but this did not prevent some six or seven thousand being present. Both side; had men off, Riley and Faulkner being away from the Run- corn team, but whilst Bradford complained in this respect, they had no cause to grumble when such players as J. Dyson, of Huddersfield, and Wilson; captain of Kendal Hornets, were introduced into the game. The play of Bradford barely came up to expectatic ns, and Runcorn were the superior combination at all points. The neat passing displays of the visitors, on more than one occasion, deserved substantial rewards; but after a determined attack had been made, Robinson got in from a loose scrimmage, which Crompton converted. With a lead of five points, the visitors resumed with a vigour that was indeed deserving of success. Bradford roused themselves near the close, and fine runs by Hawbridge and Dyson raised the seige on the Runcorn goal. Fol- lowing a run of the latter came a try by Harrison, from which Doyle landed a goal. Runcorn were severely pressed near the close, but Houghton did not belie his reputation, and defended abmirably. Strong forward rushes of the homesters were staved off with an ease which reflected credit on the Runcorn custodian, and Emmott on one occasion was almost in, the safe at- tention of S. Abrams accounting for the futile effort. It was not altogether a brilliant game, and no doubt the festive season had had its effect on the players. The visitors were very smart in the loose, their quick passing being greatly admired, and certainly deserved victory. Crompton was especially smart at centre, and Houghton was never found wanting at back. Abrams was equal to the strict attention of the Bradford halves, and all the forwards went into their work with a will and determin- ation "to leave no stone unturned" to gain the day. WIDNES v.Asputt.—This match was played at Widnes, before 2,000 spectators. The start was delayed until four o'clock,owing to the late arrival of Aspull, and only two 20's could be played. Widnes, who were poorly re- presented, kicked off. The return was a poor one, and Barber lost a chance of dropping a goal. Aspull then put Widnes on the defensive, Barber being prominent with a fine save. Once again Widnes pressed, and the forwards rushed the ball over the line, Brennan failing at goal. A foul against Aspull put an end to a dangerous rush by their front rank. Widnes, however, were some time before they got rid of their opponents, and then play was again taken to the Aspull line. Barber made an unsuccessful drop at goal, and poor play by the visit- ing back gave Widnes a lot of ground. Half time score, I Widnes 2 points Aspull nil. Final result, Widnes 16 ' points, Aspull nil.

div.head: CHESHIRE v. CUMBERLAND.
div.p: CHESHIRE v. CUMBERLAND.

The rival teams of the counties of Cheshire and Cum- berland met on Wednesday at Runcorn. The weather was of a most disagreeable character, rain falling during the whole of the time, and making the already saturated ground unfit for anything like a skilful or scientific ex- position of the game. The teams were subject to some slight alteration, the home representatives having to find substitutes for P. H. Lockwood,W. Faulkner,O. Hughes, and J. Tyack ; while the Cumberland contingent were minus Pender, of Carlisle, and Lomas, of Aspatria. The following is a complete list of the players Cheshire.—S. Houghton (Runcorn), back; F. P. Jones (New Brighton), J. H. Crompton (Runcorn), and T. H. Davie (Runcorn), three-quarters; S. Abrams (Runcorn) and F Drinkwater (Sale), half-backs;' A. J. Chadwick (Birkenhead Park), G. D. White (Birkenhead Park), H. M. Loundes (New Brighton), W. A. Williams (New Brighton), F. Little (New Brighton), W. Shaw (Run- corn), P. Riley (Runcorn), D. Massie (Runcorn), and S. F. Edmondson (Sale), forwards. Cumberland.—D. G. Lamonby (Cockermouth) back; T. Johnstone (Whitehaven), J. Sandwith (Seaton), and T. H. Hodgkinson (Carlisle), three-quarters; J. Murchie (Workington), and R. Cuthbertson (Cockermouth), half- dacks • J. Buckett, W. Leck, and J. Kidd (Millom), G. B. Atkinson (Whitehaven), J. Davidson (Aspatria), J. Moore (Workington), Brewsher (Penrith),M. Humphreys and M'Garry (Maryport), forwards. Touch judges: Messrs. Westray and H. Hughes. Re- feree: Mr. J. Payne (Lancashire County). Ten minutes after the appointed time Buckett kicked off for Cumberland, and after a spirited return by F. Jones, the ball was punted into touch by Hodgkinson at half flag. The first real scrummage, however, showed that the visitors possessed a powerful body of packers, who knew how to work, and the style in which they forced the Cheshire men back was not very comforting for the home team's supporters. Williams and Chadwick next did good work at the line out, but the fierce rush by Cumberland gained a lot of ground before Jones made a clever save. Sandwith was faulty in taking the passes made to him, but the good backing up of John- son came in very serviceable, and an assault on the I Cheshire goal ended in a dead ball. Following the drop I out Jones made a dashing run into Cumberland terri- tory before he was securely held, but all this advantage was lost when the visiting forwards broke through the scrummage, and rushed the ball to the Runcorn half Then Cumberland attacked again, and the ball was Sen• dangerously near the home line, where Davies pluckilyt got possession, and after a short run punted to the centre. Sandwith replied, and over-anxiety on Jones's part spoiled Houghton, and the game still remained in the Cheshire "25." From a loose scramble in this quarter Sandwith essayed a drop at goal, but the ball failed to rise. Crompton at last got away, but couldn't pass the opposing centre, and after Davies had been forced into touch the Runcorn captain splendidly kicked from half way into touch at the Cumberland quarter. Cheshire now seemed to have a chance, and a pretty bit of passing from Abrams to Crompton nearly resulted in the last-named getting in at the corner. Houghton failed to field the leather, but Jones was at hated, and kicked to Hodgkinson' who replied with a sprint, and was only stopped by the active exertions of Jones. From a scrummage White got away nicely and led the Cheshire forwards in an onslaught on the visitors aoal. This was repulsed in fine style, but a moment rater White, from a loose scramble, got the ball and passed to Crompton, who in turn served Davies and the latter improved the chances of Cheshire very materially. Shaw had gained some yazds a scramble near the post ended in White slipping through his opponents and

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.

The Manchester Club found Warrington more than a match for them on Saturday. For the better part of the first half the visitors played a spirited aggressive game, and at times it seemed as though they were going to carry everything before them. But they set the pace too fast, and were not able to keep it up. In the second half the " wirspullers" got the upper hand completely, and crossed the line three times. Had the game gone on much longer it would have been worse still for the Mancunians.

The Yorkshire Rugby Union Committee continue to find employment in investigating infringements of their byelaws. Castleford have been declared guilty of pro- fessionalism because they subscribed to testimonials to some of their players, and the club stands suspended to the end cf the year. The Rugby Union Committee have, at the instigation of their Yorkshire brethren, considered the question of gifts to players such as the pianoforte offered by a Leeds firm to the winners of the Yorkshire Cup. The ruling of the Committee is that such presents must be discountenanced.

It is tantalising to suffer defeat by superior place kick- ing only. This was the fate Df St. Helens at Wigan. It was a capital contest, and the Saints were unfortunate in being beaten after giving their opponents such a good game. Runcorn came very near astonishing Bradford, the latter being ia a minority of a goal until the second half was well advanced. A desperate effort enabled them to finish on level terms. It was a smart performance on behalf of the Cheshire team, despite the fact that several of the best of the Park Avenue men were absentees.

The leaders of the League had to put up with a reverse at Derby on Saturday afternoon. In view of the tre- mendous importance of the championship it was hardly worth the while of the Wanderers to arrange fora visit from Newton Heath on Christmas Day. It would have been better for them to have stored up their energies for the following day, when, as matters turned out, they were greatly needed. Derby County may not be a very formidable combination, but they have in their ranks some smart individual players, who are bound to shine when the occasion suits them. Saturday was one of their opportunities, as the hard ground was more to their taste than it was to that of the Wanderers, who could not get going in the first half. They shaped vastly different after the interval, but it was not then too late, and they were vanquished by three goals to two. The Wanderers' backs are a big heavy set of fellows and they did not show up at all well. Nothing can now keep the Dolton club at the top of the table except a series of mis- fortunes to their two closest rivals.

Preston North End have now a point better record than the Boltonians and an infinitely better goal average. They gained two points out of their return with Stoke,and yet their play was none of the best. Indeed it degenerated so much towards the close that their antagonists almost drew level. Had this occurred the Preston team would practically have been out of the running for the cup. As it is they have more than an outside chance of finishing up champions for the third time in four years. They have most to fear from Sunderland, who are at last likely to realise the high anticipations of their friends. Their ability is well knownoind if talent goes for anything the championship is a certainty for them. They seem to have fairly mastered the difficulty of playing on strange ground, and they now do almost as well away as when, at home. In this they are filling the shoes of the North End team of three years ago.

For Sunderland .to conquer Everton at Anfield Road by four goals to nothing was a very great surprise. Moreover, they were fully four goals stronger than the champions of last season. It should not be overlooked, however, that Everton early lost the services of M'Lean, one of their full backs, who was thrown down and broke his arm. This loss was seriously felt. From Evarton the Sunderland team journeyed to Wolverhampton,where they again added to their laurels, this time by three goals to one. The Wearsiders make no secret of their belie that they are at present invincible.

The Bolton Wanderers were not the only Lancashire team that suffered defeat in the Midlands. Burnley and Darwen both went through a similar experience. The Turf Moor team were on a visit to West Bromwich,where the Albion had the satisfaction of registering the only goal of the afternoon. Darwen did net escape so lightly. They were on duty at Perry Barr, and although they came off fairly well until ends were changed they were simply overwhelmed by the smart tactics of the Villa in the second half, and returned to Barley Bank beaten by 7 goals to none. Away from home the Darwen players are apparently perfectly helpless.

There is not much change to note in the position of the Alliance clubs. The Newton Heath team have lost ground somewhat, as the best they could do against the Small Heath Club was to play a draw of three geals. The match was a curiosity, inasmuch as the Birmingham team led by no fewer than three goals to none at the interval. The railway team had all the best of the game in the second half. They miss the sturdy help of Macfarlane, their captain, who is still lame. Ardwick managed to win against Grimsby Town, but were not quite class enough for Sheffield Wednesday. The latter game attracted 8,000 spectators to the ground of the Wednesday.

Bootle appear to have fallen on evil times. They lost Alliance matches on two successive days, both Walsall Town Swifts and Burton Swifts defeating them by an aggregate total of nine goals to nothing. It is rumoured that some of the Bootle players are desirous of leaving the club, and hence their indifferent form. Notts Forest, the leaders of the Alliance, were for the second time measuring their strength with their town rivals, Notts County, and were for the second time successful, in the presence of a crowd estimated at 15,000. This was a triumph for the Alliance over the League.

div.head: _ THE INDIAN CONFERENCE.
div.p: _ THE INDIAN CONFERENCE.

The Indian National Congress at the opening of Wed- nesday's sitting at Nagpur, decided to despatch a tele- gram to Mr. Gladstone, congratulating him, on entering his eighty-third year. Various resolutions were introduced affirming the necessity for the presence of elected representatives of the Indian people in the legis- lative councils, and declaring the starving condition of the masses to be largely due to the exclusion of the people from any part in the administration or in finan- cial control. A substantial reduction of the standing army, strict economy in all departments of military expenditure, and numerous other reforms are also demanded. -

The Congress held its closing sitting on Thursday. At the opening a telegram was read from General Booth, expressing sympathy with its labours. A reply was voted, thanking the General and gratefully acknowledg- ing the good work being done by the Salvation Arrny in India. After various other resolutions had been passed the Congress dissolved with enthusiastic cheers for the Queen, Empress of India;

div.head: RUNCORN VACCTNATION OFFICER- .
div.p: RUNCORN VACCTNATION OFFICER- .

A letter was read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the re-arrangement of the relief districts of Runcorn? Frodsham, and Budworth, and forwarding a form to be filled up with regard to Mr. Ward's appoint- ment as vaccination officer for Runcorn. After some discussiom the clerk was•empowered to fill up the form, and the fee of Mr. Ward for each successful vaccination was fixed at 5c1., an the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Aaron. This it was stated would amount to ahout £l5 a year, the same amount paid to Mr. Col- burn, the former vaccination officer.

div.head: TEE COUNTY COITECIL,PRIICEPT.
div.p: TEE COUNTY COITECIL,PRIICEPT.

The Clerk reported that he had received a precept from the County Council for £3,291 ss. id. to be paid on January 30th.—Mr. Taylor; Is that all p—Mr. Heywood: What is our balance in the hank ?—Mr. Brandreth : We can do it.—Mr. Aaron : I suppose they have not sent us word how they had spent it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Tay- lor : They want to spend it. (Laughter.)—Mr. Aaron : They must have spent it or they would not ask for it.— The Chairman : You will get a balance sheet when it is published.—Mr. Btandreth said as they had a County Councillor on the Board he would see that a copy of the balance sheet be sent to every guardian in the Union.— Mr. Speakman : Then we should' have complaints from the. ratepayers that the rates were getting up very high.—Mr. Heywood : Tho Council can afford to send us a big book with regard to the charities, which was really only a rough draught, but which must have cost a large sum of money, and I don't see why they cannot send us a balance sheet.—Mr. Brandreth : I think we Guardians ought to have one.—Mr. Speakman : Therois one Commissioner here and I think by resolution of the Bbard any member might have one for a week, and pass it on.—Mr. Ed- wards : I don't think a circulating library like Mr. Speakman talks of would be acceptable. (Laughter.)— Mr. Speakman : Anything I can, do to get the Guardians a copy I shall only be too pleased.—Mr. Brandreth said Runcorn Union paid the Council £8;600. a year, and surely the 42 Guardians of' the. Union could have a balance sheet to show how the money had been spent. He moved that the County Council be requested to send each Guardian a copy of the balancesheet of the county when oublished.—Mr. Edwards seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Heywood; Mr. Speakman will support, I hope.—Mr: Speakman Yes, I shall have very great pleasure.

div.head: LINAICER'S CLAIM.
div.p: LINAICER'S CLAIM.

A letter was read from Mr. H. G: Linaker, of Frod- sham, suggesting that his claim should bo referred to arbitration, and after some discussion MY. Baxter gave notice that he would move a resolution to this effect at the next meeting. It was also understood that in the meantime Mr. Baxter would see Mr. Linaker with a view to a compromise.

div.head: FINANCE. -SCHOOL INQUIRY OFFICERS:
div.p: FINANCE. -SCHOOL INQUIRY OFFICERS:

Mr. Brandreth moved the payment of accounts amounting to upwards of eleven hundred pounds and said this was about £240 more than the corresponding period last year. The increase was caused in the House. Butcher's meat had cost' £s' more, there was an increase of £5 in milk, £lO in groceries, £l4 in coal, £lO in clothing, in potatoes £3O. They had however a large stock of coal and potatoes in advance. An increase of £23 in boots had been caused through Mr. Dansey, the Local Government Board inspector, compelling the Master to provide each boy with two pairs. There was a heavy item of £44 from Messrs. Timmins for a cooking range and from Mr. Davies, of Frodsham, of L2T for a fire escape, both of which the Local Government Board had ordered. There was one item he had objected to for some time and that was £l7 10s. for school inquiry officers for Runcorn, seeing that they were only paid in school pence about 2s. 3d. a week. They ought to get rid of this charge at once, and if the Guardians for Rtincorn would put a little energy into the affair this would be done.—The Clerk said the Local Government Bbard would not dispense with these officers until full reasons were given.—Mr. Haywood suggested that Mr. Ward the relieving officer could do the work in conjunction with his school attendance work for an increased salary it was proposed to give for the latter.—Mr. Taylor said he should not support such a proposal. He strongly ob- jected to parents applying for school fees, being tainted with pauperism.—Mr. Speakman suggested that Mr. Bowyer the school yisitor should be appointed, but the Chairman ruled that they could not deal with the sub- ject that day.—Mr. Speakman gave notice that he would bring the subject forward at the next meeting and in the meantime the Runcorn Guardians would consider the question and be prepared with a recom- mendation.

div.head: ISM. PIERPOINT'S lIIMITEIST.
div.p: ISM. PIERPOINT'S lIIMITEIST.

The Clerk reported that the bequest of the late Mr Pierpoint, of Runcorn, had been distributed to 100' poor. persons who had received 23. each.—Mr. Taylor said he and Mr. Lea were present when relief was distributed at Runcorn, on Thursday,and they gave 23. to each of those who were considered the most deserving. He suzgestcd that a list of the names should be forwarded to Mr. Pier- pilot's relatives.—Mr. Speakman proposed that this should be done and that Mr. Taylor and Mr. Lea be thanked for kindly dolinr, out the bequest.--Mr. Ed wards seconded.—Carried.' INCREASE OF OFFICER'S SALARIES, .
Mr. Aaron gave notice that at the next meeting he should move increases in the salaries of the School Atten- dance Officers of the Union.

ABSOLUTE PERFECTION. The Chairman asked the Master (Mr. Cunnah) if he could give any information as to the spirits used in, the house.—The Master said he could not give the exact amount without consulting his book, but there was very little granted, and always on the recommendation of the Medical Officer. Up to the previous day two,ounces a day were givan.—Mr. Speakman said they were then absolute perfection, so far as drink was concerned. Nothing given except ordered by the doctor.—The Master : Only in extreme cases.

div.head: CIIRISTMAS IN THR
div.p: CIIRISTMAS IN THR

The Master reported that the inmates had their banal treat on Christmas day, and in the evening an entertain- ment was given by the officers and children. The chapel and dining room had been decorated for the festive season by the officers. Mrs. Marsden, of Sutton, had sent Christmas letters • Mr. Kydd, Frodsham, sweets); Mrs. Wright, Halton, 'Christmas cards ; and Mr. Talbot, Dutton Lodge. evergreens. Tobacco for the smokers and oranges, nuts, and currant bread for the children had been provided by money subscribed by Guardians.

div.head: ANNUAL RAGGED • SCHOOL, TREAT.
div.p: ANNUAL RAGGED • SCHOOL, TREAT.

The annual Christmas treat to the children at- tending the Warrington Ragged School, was given in the Drill Hall, on Saturday afternoons The flags which had been put up for the volunteer prize dis- tribution, which took place on Christmas Eve, re- mained there, and imparted a somewhat more pic- turesque character to the occasion than would otherwise have been the case. The expense of the treat, we may remind our readers, is annually de- frayed by public subscription, and some few of the subscribers, when it comes off, usually make their appearance to satisfy themselves with witnessing the dispensation of their charity ; this being the case on Saturday. About 1,400 children were pre- sent; and, judging from the extraordinary excite- ment and animation which prevailed amonest them, one might fairly pronounce that the treat was appreciated by them in a pre-erninent degree. Each of the juveniles on entering received a paper bag containing a piece of currant bread, a bun, and bread and jam,the elder children having in addition an extra bun or scone. Tea and milk were subse- quently supplied by way of liquid refreshment. It may be remarked that considering the class of children for whom the treat was provided, there was a surprising comparative absence of that tatterdemalion element one might have expected to see, many of the juveniles, in- deed being quite decently clothed. Amongst the ladies and gentlemen present were Mr. J. Skelland, superintendent of the Ragged School, Mr. J. Owen, assistant superintendent, Mr. J. Welsby, treasurer, and Mr. E. Osborne, financial secretary ; Messrs. Thos. Woods, H. Osborne, Johnston., John- son Maybury, Garland, F. Davison, W. Rodgers- and Owen ; and Mesdames Welsby, Osborne, John, son, Bayley, hawrenson, Howard, Maybury, Wood- house, and Rodgers, Miss Mason, Miss Pemberton, and Sergeant-Major Burns. Mrs. Howard's class of elder girls and Mr. H. Osborne's class of elder boys, assisted in the distribution of the meat. it had been intended to give a magic lantern exhibi- tion to the children,but the Committee had not been able to bring this about. When the children had come to the close of what was an extraordinarily demonstrative discussion of the good things pro- vided for them, a hearty vote of thanks was ac- corded, on the motion of Mr. Skelland, econdo.-1 by Mr. Owen, to those who organised the gathering, and assisted in carrying out the treat, and to the subscribers. Mr. Thomas Woods afterwards ad- dressed a few encouraging remarks to the children, who on their departure from the hall had an orange handed to each of them; and they then scampered merrily homewards.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL. DISASTER AT GATESHE AD.
div.p: FRIGHTFUL. DISASTER AT GATESHE AD.
CRY OF FIRE IN. TWAT RE. A PANIC AND LOSS +or lIEN LIVES.

A frightful disaster, one stiela as frequently accom- panies the season's festivities, .occurred at Gateshead on Saturday evening, when, at the Theatve Royal, a panic entailed the death of ten people under most harrowing circumstancest

The lessee of the Gateshead Trieatre•Royal, which is a minor playhouse, had on Christmas, Eve produced his pantomime, entitled " Aladdinrwittr a most encourag- ing result. Oh the night of Boxing Div, a holiday audience, numbering about twelve hundred, assembled, filling thespacious gallery and pit to nverflowing, whilst the other parts of the house were numerously occupied. As the pantomirse progressed, the greatest good humour prevailed in the house, and it was in the opening of the last scene," The Great Wall of China;': that the incident occurred which: was fraught with, such terrible I and fatal consequences. In the lower cirole, on the left-hand side facing the stage,. a woman, who was accompanied by her husbaud,'. dropped either a scarf pin or a fibrin piece on the fleor. Be, without thought of any dangerew m that might be caused by the act, struck a match and t'looked for the missing article. By some means or other apiece of paper onthellbor caught fire, and the paper and sawdust smouldering together caused a flame which, though slight, was sufficient to alarm the woman, who called out "Fire." A, hand was put across her mouth to prevent a repetition of the words which have so often before caused panic,. but again the cry was heard of "-Fire, fire," and as a volume of smoke was now curling upwards, the alarm spread at once, and the audience starbsd to its feet and made straightway for the exits. On the stage Mr. Turner-and hia company realizing at once the dread nature of the rush, and also the smallness of the fire, called on 'the audience to keep their places or go out in order. The injunc- tions were, however, wasted and as seine of the pit occupants went back to the ordinary exits, crowds tore down the orchestra partition and clamber- ing on the stage, swarmed out at the nar ow private staircase. From the lower circle the r pie got out safely, but numbers preferred to-lower ism- selves or jump to the pit ; whilst from the gar y, at the edge nearest the stage, the more ven,.. esome jumped direct to the stage. In the meantime, the bulk of the gallery audience made its way to the one exit, and here a three-quarter door was bolted: Fbater, the check-taker in charge, managed eventually to draw the bolt, releasing the door, but the acticost hinshis life, for before he could leave the place the -weight of the surging] crowd forced him down and it is not supposed that he ever again regained his feet. Three stairs to a landing form the way to the main staircase, and it would anpear that in their haste to leave the theatre those who pressed onwards, stumbled down the three I stairs, and were failtln upon by the masa behind, and I the means of egress thus became greatly impeded, though hundreds found their way down do the street without hurt. When the people ceased to 'our down the stairs, it was assumed by Ore excited populace in' the streets surrounding the Theatre Royal that all had emerged, but as Thomas Butler and Thomas Gordon were ascending the gallery stairs, they were horrified to fine a wall of living and dead people to a height of five feet, whilst behind them there still struggled those who had not been able to proceed further up to • that time. With assistance they pulled out men, lads, and girls, most of whom were suffering from shock, whilst othrs were more dead than alive, and did not long survive when carried to neighbouring houses. It was about half-past ten o'clock when the catastrophe took place, and in a few minutes the fire had been extin- guished, with the aid'of a few buckets of water. Before eleven o'clock death had ensued in several cases, an' before midnight there had been ten deaths, whilst at Newcastle Royal Infirmary patients had been admitted suffering from shock and bruises. Nine of the dead bodies were removed to the Temperance HMI adjoining where they were identified during Sunday mcrning—the scenes being heartrending. The names of the girl, men, and lads killed are appended :

div.p: TERRIBLE' BIITCET.ERY /N,- YEMEN.

SIEGE OF A CITY BY FORTY THOUSAND ARABS. Wednesday night's "Pall Mall Gazette" had the fol- lowing :—The siege of the city of Sana, Yemen, by the Arab insurgents, began on the 14th July and ended on the 10th October; and more than 40,000 insurgents took part in it. While the besiegers kept up a continual bombardment, a terrible famine prevailed. EVery man who left the city had his nose or ears cut off; and was driven back to Sana naked as a hand. The TUrkish gar- rison of the town behaved splendidly, for though officers and men were 'half-starved they were on the walls day and night, and kept the enemy under control. The chief of the insurgents was Mollah Salah Eodin4 a native of the city of Saacinh, who proclaimed all over the country that he would' convert the 60,000 .Jews of Yemen to Islam or would extirpate them. During the last days of the siege the insurgents had approached 'the city within 1,000 feet. On October 10th a Turkish army of relief appeared, and seen got the mastery of the insurgents. On the follbwing evening the Turkish commander, Achmed Feiti Pasha, entered the city in triumph, where he was welcomed as a saviour, especially by the Jews. No quarter-was given to prisoners either by the Turks or by the insurgents, and so the battle was, followed by a. terrible butchery.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN SCOTLAND+

On• Saturday night, the passenger train from Glasgow. to Lesmahagow ran off the rails at Haughead Junction 4 on the Caledonian Railway, and nine persons were more or less.seriously injured.the worst cases being Mrs. Park, William Graham, and William Frew. The accident oc- curred at a sharp curve where the Motherwell andlLes- mahagow branches diverge. A similar accident occurred at the same place two, years ago, when the curve was straightened to 901110 extent, and deemed quite safe. The dtiver and stoker saved their lives by jumping off; but they suffered from severe shock. Some of tne passengers ran back to Hamilton, and medical aid was soon forth- coming. The two.,,Park and Prow, amongst the worst hurt, were conveyed to their homes' ten mildistant ; a man named Graham was taken to his son's house, and the others were able to proceed home.

div.p: THE BRIGHTON MUMMER..

At Brighton on Wednesday, George Henry Wood, railway servant, was again brought before the magis- trates charged with wilfully murdering the little girl Edith Jeal. On prisoner being placed in the dock, Mr. Pope, whanrosecuted, said that Dr. Stevenson,to whom the clothes worn by the accused had been sent, would state that the accused's trousers were considerably bloodstained, and that there were also blood stains upon his flannel shirt and woollen drawers. At the, close of the evidence the prisoner was committed for trial.

THE PEARL CASE.

Sir,—As several statements have appeared in the Public Press respecting this case, which might seriously injure our reputation, we shall feel obliged if you will kindly allow us, in justice to ourselves, to correct them. The facts of the case are these. The portion of Mrs. Hargreave's jewels purchased by us for £550 were valued by herself at not more than, £3OO, which, taking into consideration that they were 'second-hand articles, may, we venture to think, be considered a fair price for us to have given. The sum of £5,000 which has been erroneously applid to the jewels in question was the value which Major Hargreave (in evidence at the recent trial) placed upon the whore of his wife's jewels—plainly a very different thin,. We should like to add that the report in some of the morning papers of to-day that we are prosecuting Mrs. Osborne is not correct.—We are, sir, yours faithfully, SPINK & SON.
1 & 2, Gracechurch-St., Cornhill, London, EC., 28th Dec., 1891.
NEWTON GUARDIANS AND CHRISTMAS BOXES
FOR THE POOR.

Sir,—l presented on behalf of Messrs. Hood-Wright and Hibbert(Guardians)the sum of one shilling to each of the poor in receipt of relief,to the number of eleven,who assembled at the Town Hall, Newton, on Christmas Eve. All of the recipients were loud in their exclamations of thanks to the donors.

On this morning Mr. George Ratcliffe of Earlestown presented to each of the poor, to the number of 30, who assembled at the Earlestown pay station for their relief with a large currant loaf. Each person thanked Mr. Ratcliffe for his kindness and generosity. I publish this not for the sake of praising the givers, but having heard a remark that the guardians were generous at Christmas time with the public funds, I therefore take the opportunity of informing the public that what waA given by the gentlemen named, was given from their own private income.—l am, Sir, yours truly,

sir.—The idea a good one, idea of c.r:itiCi-s'in-g-o—u-r—lloe-a-1:--1";:rliament is in opinio as it has a tendency to en- lighten the inhabitants and to induce them to think for themselves, and take a more active part in the business of the town thin heretofore. A little wholesome criti- cism is also beneficial to those gentlemen who are acting on the Board, and managing the public business. The opportunities to discuss imperial questions are ample, and Ido not know why our local questions should not be as fully ventilated. All the inhabitants are interested irectly or indirectly, and no one should stand aside. Mr. Thompson is the nail the majority of your corres- pondents are hitting on the bead, but I should be sorry to strike a blow at it, for knowing Mr. Thompson as I do lam convinced that his well known good nature and simplicity have gained for him notoriety that he would gladly dispense with, and I haTe no doubt that he will take the advice given him, and resign. If he do this, his mistake will soon be forgotten. I notice the compliment paid to Mr. Emmett, by one

of your correspondents, and when it is recollected what a muddle the gas management got into, through the incompetency and temporary popularity of the late Chairman of the Gas Committee, and how ably Mr. Emmett took it out of his hands and put the matter right, I think lie deserves the compliment. I know perfectly well that Mr. Emmett has also done good ser- vice in other matters, but when he comes forward and tells the ratepayers, through the press, that the Commis- sioners have decided to increase the expenditure on the Public Hall by £2,700 at a bound, for the sole reason that the clerk had overgrown his clothes, the subterfuge is so apparent that the inhabitants refuse to accept the statement even when made by the Chairman of Commis- sioners supported, as it was, by Mr. Ratcliffe. It might be worth Mr. Emmett's while to keep in mind when dealing in this high-handed way with the Town Hall business, that there are others who can ap- proach the Chairman and Directors of the Railway Co. Lord Stalbridge is at the head of an immense staff of clerks and others, and perhaps no one is better qualified to judge as to the space required by the Newton Com- missioners for their clerk and boy. If there be a clique, I am reluctantly compelled to believe that Mr. Emmett knows something about it. It would appear that a few of his workmen met him and asked him to do certain things, at the next Commissioners' meeting. He appears and makes a speech to the inhabitants that a deputation of the ratepayers has waited upon him and asked him to take tile chair for another year. There is something very unsatisfactory in this, and an explanation is needed. If longer withheld, it is possible it may be obtained from another quarter. December 29th, 1891.
CRITIC.
THE DOCTRINES OF THE CHURCH.

Sir,—Kindly allow me to reply to J.T.C.C. and Wm. oulton, in yours of Saturday. J.T.C.C. quotes Acts 14c. 22v. for "priests." On looking at it there is no such word. I find disciples but not priests; in the bllowing verse he will find "elders in every church." Note more than one. The Christian ministry does not contain a priest (Sacerdos) sacrifices for sin being at an end after Christ once offered himself, once for all, never to be re- peated. Christ is our great High Priest, ever living, and his priesthood is not transmittable. (See Heb. 7c. 24- 28vs.) If J.T.C.C. will look at my letter, he will see "diocesan bishop." I ask him to find me such an official in the New Testament. He cannot. If I grant• him his argument, perhaps he will tell me how comes it to pass there were bishops (note plural) in the church at Phillippi (see lc. Iv.) We read of "overseers," " elders," "ministers," "pastors," but of "priests "never. Presbyter is priest writ large, and priest is presbyter writ small ; so says the late Dean Hook, and so also the late Holy Smith, rector of Tansley. I advise J.T.C.C. to read his work "High Church " ; Archbishop Cranmer wrote : Bishops and priests were not two things, but one office in the beginning of Christ's religion (Works page 117, Parker Society). Bishop Jewell said the same. There are only two orders in the Christian Church, viz., elders and deacons. I have qupted three of the highest authorities in the,Church of England, showing that, bishop, elder, presbyter, or priest are terms used for one individual. . .

Of course J.T.C.C. and W. Poulton must have a priest, or they could have no low or high mass, for both teach that Christ is priest and victim in the Eucharist, see Hymns A. & M. 316, 4v., a statement denied in Hebrews Bc. 4v. I pointed out that the Prayer Book in the Communion office does not contain the word altar, but Table, yet J.T.C.C., has the audacity to re- peat the word Altar. Church decorations come from Paganism ; see Hone's Every Day Book, vol. 1, and Blackie's Encyclopedia. Christ ascended into Heaven on purpose to send the Holy Spirit the Comforter. We are told that when He comes again every eye shall see Him. Does J.T.C.C. or V.P., see Him on Christmas Day? Such assertions, practically deny the presence of the Comforter. How is it W.P., jumps away from infant baptism IF he will look into his Douay Bible, with Leo Haydock's notes, he will find the ancient custom was immer- sion of believers not infants. The apostles called on men to repent, to believe in Christ, and be bap- tised ; and they baptised, not sprinkled, none but those who appeared to them to be true believers, Acts 2c. 33, 47, 16c., 31v., 18., Bv. The late Bishop J. B. Lightfoot, of Durham, in Col. 2c. 12v. wrote : "It was the baptism of believers (not infants) by immersion." Bishop Burnet says : " Teaching must precede baptism." Dr. R. P. Blakeney wrote: " Con- firmation was not instituted by Christ or his apostles, in the Church of England ; it is merely an ecclesiastic ordinance." Bishop Jewell said similar. Alex. Hales, an eminent schoolman wrote : " The Sacrament of con- firmation, as it is a Sacrament, was not ordained in the council of Melda. The Ritualists and Romanists tell us that confirmation makes us perfect Christians." Why, on the last occasion here, after Bishop Jayne had put his hands on mere children, I asked two lads about the Lord's Supper and the 39 articles, and they were completely ignorant. Cranmer says : "There is no place in scripture that declareth the sacrament to be institute of Christ." (Works p. 80.) The Church of England does not teach Auricular confession. The pas- sage in James sc. 16 v. quoted by W. P. will prove too much for him ; his priest according to this is bound to tell his faults to W. P. He quotes in John 20 c. 23v., but omits the first word in next verse. The key to this disputed text is to be found in Luke 24 c. 18-47 v. and Acts 1c.15 v. It was the power of the preached word that was to remit sins or return sins to those who heard the message of salvation, and believed it or rejected it, (see John 12c. 48v.) W. P. cannot prove that from the Pope down to the last made deacon, they are what they profess to be owing to the Doctrine of Intention. If he will study this, he will cease to uphold popery,which is not Christi- anity. John H. Newman (afterwards Cardinal) wrote in tract xx. " The Roman communion is infected with heresy ;we are bound to flee it as a pestilence. They have established a lie in place of God's truth, and by their claim to immutability in doctrine, cannot undo the sin they have committed!' Personal abuse is not argu- ment.—Yours &c. Frodsham, December 29,1891.
ROBERT FOULKES.

SCIENCE AND SENTIMENT: A NEW ANALOGY BY A NEW BUTLER. I have many other ways to die ; meantime, laugh at his challenge." (Antony and Cleopatra) 4.-1. Sir,—lnasmuch as I can conceive many pleasanter ways of dying than being talked to death, I must decline to discuss with Mr. W. H. Butler the question of the genesis life, or that of the mind. I decline to open such a discussion for these very sufficient reasons: Firstly, I am not fitted, either by having sufficient knowledge or inclination, for such a task ; and again, if undertaken, it would lead to no good result, but would be a mere waste of time and type. Such a subject is quite out of the range of practical science ; it is in the domain of speculation—of philosophic hypothesis. I have not sufficient data upon which to found an argument of any practical value. Mr. W. H. Butler may have, but if so, he stands unique among men. Ido not think Herbert Spencer himself, perhaps the best authority we have on this subject, would consent to fight upon this attenuated battle-ground. But, greatly daring, Mr. Butler, in the plentitude of his knowledge, throws down the glove. Bye the way —is it a a glove or a gauntlet? Mr. Butler's metaphors are rather mixed. In the same sentence, I am Appolyon " seeking whom I may devour and running a tilt at every windmill I come across." Now Mr. Butler may thank his stars that he is not a wind- mill and that I have neither time nor inclination to prick every Self-inflated wind-bag I may come across. I am not so far gone in Quixotism as to be unable to distinguish between Mambrino's helmet on a wise head and a barber's basin as the head-piece of windy verbo. ity. It is for such that Ireserve the "gall" he speaks of. Flippart irrelevancies and argument by evasion deserve such bitter treatment. But while declining to open a discussion on this subject, I will engage to show his deficiencies and failures, if he will undertake to furnish the materials for so much fun. He has heard of Icarus ; let him beware ot the sun.. Your correspondent displays in the selection of his subject, a want of knowledge or a want of judgment. ' If he knew it to be, as it is, a mere matter of speculative ' opinion, why should he wish to raise upon it what must be a fruitless and unprofitable discussion ? At present the world is all too young in biological knowledge to furnish materials enough to make this a theme for prac- tical debate. But, as Mr. Butler appears to wish to pose as the champion of orthodoxy, or as council for defend- ent in the case of Science versus Sentiment, I can "find him some work "nearer home, than on the out of way platform he proposes to figure upon. Work too, as being applicable to the wants and wishes of living men and women,crving aloud for present consideration. Now I claim to have a higher motive in writing than the display of a certain amount of mere scribbling ability my endeavour has everbeen to uphold what I conceived to be the truth, and to show the unreasonablenese of what I thought was error. Now there is an error very prevalent among us and one like most errors, entailing pernicious consequences. Though handed down from barbaric ages, we still in our semi-barbaric darkness, hug to our bosoms the tradition of man's original per- fection. Now if there is any reliance to be put on the results of human investigation—any faith to be placed in the logical deduction frimi well-ascertained facts- - N G

the origin of man was just the very reverse of this—a slow progressive, evolutionary process from non-human, through the semi-human into the human type. The earliest traces we have of man upon earth show him to have been a low-type savage ; so says, science. Sentiment will have it that he was created perfect. Here then we have a definite issue, and if Mr. Butler wishes to cover himself with glory as the David of orthodoxy by slaying the Goliah of unbe- lief, let him see to his sling—gather up his pebbles—slay the unholy giant, and wear upon his modest brow the laurels of successful polemics. Using his own language "I hope," Mr. Butler" will be able to see his way to taking up this subject." Better this by far than attempt- ing his plan, which might be paralleled by one attempt- ing the Integral calculus, whilst ignorant of arithmetic. To show the practical side of such a discussion, let me say that I have a firmly rooted belief that the general acceptance of evolution, as a working day creed would be beneficial to mankind morally and intellectually. By showing men that they were not the degraded and degrad- ing beings they had been taught to believe themselves, but had within themselves the spring and fountain of mental improvement, thus opening out fresh fields for self-culture, and so encouraging them to strive to preserve this innate blessing and increase its flow. What improvement has hitherto been effected has been in spite of—rather than with the assistance of—this pessimistic doctrine. Note the denuncia- tion of the use of the reasoning faculties by some 'of its professors—when the reasoning went against them. Herein they showed the inherent weakness of their cause; for assuredly any cause in which reason- ing is inadmissible must itself be unreasonable. "I am amused, and I must confess it," at Mr. Butler's ready assumption that "If the whole of living nature and the whole domain of mind are to be referred to purely material causes then there is no room or reason for God. Here our critic talks like a child. Surely one who wants to dispute upon Abiogenesis ought to know that every ' forward step of science has been met in the same way. As science advances the man-formed-idea of God recedes, but ccmmensurate with the recession the idea is enobled and enlarged. From the savage who can make a god to the philosopher who cannot even conceive the idea,there are many steps, but they have been taken.—l am. &e. JOHN PEERS. Penketh, Dec. 27th, 1891.

Redmond, who was returned for Waterford last ,lder son of a former M.P., for Wexford,a constituency which he himself sat for until a few , months back, when he re- signed in order to contest the seat in Cork rendered vacant iy the death of Mr. Parnell. Ithough still only 35 or 36 'ears of age, he has tor several ?ears taken a prominent part in Irish political movements. ';o far back as 1883, he visited

A, was warmly received by the Irish with National sympathies, and that visit was the means of pouring into the coffers of the National League quite £lO,OOO. But while doing splendidly for the Irish party in Australia Mr. Redmond did well for himself, for he captured a wife in the person of the handsome daughter of a wealthy Australian. At the time of the great diversion of the Irish party Mr. Redmond strongly expoused the cause of Mr. Parnell, and was generally looked upon as the "chief's " principal lieutenant. Upon the demise of Mr. Parnell, Mr. Redmond was formally installed as the leader of the Parnellite party. At the same time he resigned his own seat iu Parliament for Wexford,for the pur- pose of contesting the seat in Cork formally held by Mr. Parnell. In that contest he was, however, signally defeated. Nevertheless, he has, as all now know, been more fortunate at Waterford. Speaking at a meeting of the Irish National League, held in Dublin, on Tuesday, Mr. John Red- mond, M.P., said he believed his recent victory at Waterford was the b.ginning of the revival of the Parnellite party in Ireland, whose prospects were particularly bright and favourable.

div.head: INFLUENZA.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA.

Whole families are being stricken down by influenza in the Ashford and Elham districts. At a meeting of the local Board of Guardians on Thursday, it was decided at the instance of Dr. Robinson East, the Kent medical officer, to issue a warning to persons suffering from the epidemic not to expose themselves in public under a pexalty of £5.

-----.- SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A PUBLICAN.

On Thursday Morning, M. S. Brighouse, county I coroner, held an inquiry at the Cock and Trumpet Inn, Ilalewood, near Widnes, relative to the death of Richard Whitfield, My-eight years of age, licensed victualler, of the Beehive Inn, Halewood. A married daughter of the deceased stated that her mother died in June last, and this had had a very depressing effect upon her father. She gave him his breakfast in bed, and he then complained of pains in his head. He got up shortly after eleven o'clock. About twenty minutes to twelve she missed him, and, on going in search for him, she found him in the wash-house on his hands and knees. His throat was cut, and an open razor covered with blood was lying on the floor. She got assistance, and he was carried into the house. Dr. Hutchinson, of Widnes, was called in, and he at- tended him up to his death, which took place on Wednesday morning. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

div.p: PENKETIL

bITDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD. On New Year's Eve Mrs. Parker,wife of Mr. Chas. Edward Parker, of Vine House, Penketli, was called out cf a watch night service at Penketh Wesleyan Chapel to attend to her infant son Chas.. Parker, aged nine months, who she was informed was alarmingly ill. She hurried home just in time to be present at her son's death. The child had been a healthy infant, and she had left it at home that evening perfectly well. The suddeness of its death was therefore all the greate: shock to the parents.

TEA PARTY AND ENTERTAINMENT. On Thursday evening in connection with the Wesleyan Sunday School, the usual New Year's Eve tea party and entertainment were held in the schoolroom. There was a large number present, the room being crowded. The tea, which was prepared by the lady teachers of the school in their usual ex- cellent manner, was much appreciated. After tea the entertainment was held, Mr. C. E. Parker pre- siding over the meeting. The programme, which consisted of songs, anthems, part-songs, pianoforte duets, violin and flute duets, accordeon solos, dia- logues, readings, recitations, &c., was executed in a most praiseworthy manner and well received.At the close of the entertainment, supper was served for Those staying the watchnight services, which was conducted by the Rev. T. Ross. There was a good attendance.

A CONVEMSAZIONE. In connection with the Muturd Improvement Association the annual conversazione was- held on Wednesday evening. There was a good attendance. The schoolroom had been very tastefully decorated for the occasien with mottoes, evergreens, Sec., and presented a most pleasing appearance. The presi- dent of the association (Mr. T. Gandy) presided over the evenings entertainment. A miscellaneous programme consisting of vocal and instrumental music was gone through and much appreciated, Mrs. C. E. Parker accompanying the pieces on the piano in a very able manner. A magic lantern exhibition was given by Mr. R. E. Garnett,the slides being of a miscellaneous character. Mr. Peers also explained the new method of developing photograph negatives by the kallitype process. During the evening re- freshments were handed round and greatly appre- ciated, everyone doing full justice to them. They were prepared by Mrs. T. Gandy, Miss Moses, Miss Hilda, and Miss Garnett. At the close of the en- tertainment, games were commenced and indulged in till 11 o'clock. The proceedings concluded with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.p: LYMM.

-- THE LABOUR QUESTION.—The members of the P.S.A. services at the Congregational Church were given an address by Mr. James Dodds, on Sunday afternoon, on some phases of the labour question. The speaker, who iS well qualified to speak en labour subjects.was listened to attentively by a large congregation of working-men. Lymar DIVIDEN/t•SOCIETY (ROSE IN THE VALLEY).—The annual audit of the above society took place on Monday at the Lodge-room, Bull's Hewl Hotel, by Messrs. James Hall and Mark Winstanley. Mr. G. H. Leigh,. the sec., in giving in his report for the past year, said he was sorry he could not declare so large a dividend as last o year, this being his 25th year as their secretary. This oi was the heaviest year, with the exception of two, of [ sickness during that period ; but, on the ther hand, there had been no deaths during the year to record, and that the funeral fund and contingent fund would be I banked during next week.

--- SHEPHERDS BY NIGHT LODGE, LYSIM, LOYAL ORDER OP ANCIENT SHIIPHERDS.—The audit of the above society took place on Wednesday, when Mr. AleNander Oliver of Heaton Mersey, and Mr. Jas. Astley attended to audit the books. Mr. George E. Leigh gave his report for the past year. He had great pleasure in saying the latter half of the year had been one of success, both numeri- cally and financially. He was also pleased to inform them that there had been no deaths during the year, and to inform them that during the past month they had initiated two honorary members in the lodge, and he hoped others would follow. The auditors congratulated , the secretary and Mr. Robert Ditchteld, the treasurer, on the neat way they kept their respective books.
